Reduce the PI‑LL mismatch to less than 10°
items.e: Schwab's realignment targets are PI–LL within about 10°, SVA under 5 cm and PT under 20°. Residual PI–LL mismatch is associated with poor outcomes, persistent pain and junctional failure.

items.q: In the SRS–Schwab classification of adult spinal deformity, a pelvic tilt of 25° is given which modifier?
items.e: SRS–Schwab PT modifiers are 0 (under 20°), + (20–30°) and ++ (over 30°); the same grading applies to PI–LL (under 10°, 10–20°, over 20°) and SVA (under 4 cm, 4–9.5 cm, over 9.5 cm). There is no +++ grade.

items.q: The most common pattern of meniscal tear in a young athlete after a sudden change of direction is:
items.e: In young athletes, twisting injuries (often with ACL tears) produce vertical longitudinal tears, which can become bucket-handle tears. Horizontal cleavage and complex tears are degenerative patterns in older patients.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a recognised risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip in neonates?
items.e: Established DDH risk factors include female sex, breech presentation, positive family history, first-born, oligohydramnios and other packaging disorders (torticollis, metatarsus adductus). In-utero steroid exposure is not a risk factor.

items.q: The most appropriate first‑line investigation for a 5‑day‑old with a suspected unilateral hip dislocation is
items.e: Ultrasound is the modality of choice for hips <6 months of age; it visualises the cartilaginous structures and detects dislocation without radiation.

items.q: On the AP pelvis of a 2-year-old with DDH, the ossific nucleus of the femoral head lies lateral to Perkin's line but below the level of the superolateral acetabular margin. The Tönnis grade is:
items.e: In Tönnis grading by position of the ossific nucleus, grade I is medial to Perkin's line, II is lateral to Perkin's line but below the superolateral acetabular margin, III is at the level of the margin, and IV is above it. The IHDI classification uses the metaphyseal midpoint for infants without a nucleus.

items.q: Which of the following statements about the use of the Pemberton osteotomy in treatment of DDH is TRUE?
o: It is indicated after closure of the triradiate cartilage
It is an incomplete transiliac osteotomy hinging on the triradiate cartilage that reduces acetabular volume
It is a complete osteotomy that always needs internal fixation
It is first-line treatment for neonatal DDH
items.e: The Pemberton pericapsular osteotomy hinges on the open triradiate cartilage (age about 18 months to 6–8 years) and bends the roof anterolaterally, reducing the volume of a capacious acetabulum. It is stable without fixation, unlike the Salter osteotomy, which hinges at the symphysis.

items.q: In an infant treated with a Pavlik harness for DDH, forced hip abduction beyond the 'safe zone' mainly risks:
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Pavlik harness disease (posterior acetabular wall erosion)
items.e: Excessive abduction compresses the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery, causing AVN. Excessive flexion causes femoral nerve palsy and inferior dislocation. Pavlik harness disease results from keeping a persistently dislocated hip in the harness beyond 3–4 weeks.

items.q: A 34-year-old woman has a painful bunion. Weight-bearing radiographs show a hallux valgus angle of 22°, an intermetatarsal angle of 11° and a congruent joint without arthritis. The most appropriate procedure is:
o: Distal chevron osteotomy of the first metatarsal
items.e: Mild hallux valgus (HVA under about 20–25°, IMA under about 13°) is corrected by a distal chevron osteotomy. Proximal osteotomies and Lapidus are for larger IMA or hypermobility, and MTP arthrodesis is for arthritis or severe or neuromuscular deformity.

items.q: A 15-year-old girl has forefoot pain under the second ray. Radiographs show flattening and sclerosis of the second metatarsal head. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Freiberg infraction is osteonecrosis of the lesser metatarsal head (second most often), typically in adolescent girls. Köhler disease affects the navicular, Iselin disease the base of the fifth metatarsal apophysis, and Sever disease the calcaneal apophysis.

items.q: A 15-year-old has a diaphyseal femoral lesion with a permeative pattern and onion-skin periosteal reaction. Which histological finding is most characteristic of Ewing sarcoma?
o: Sheets of small round blue cells with strong membranous CD99 staining
Storiform spindle cells with giant cells
items.e: Ewing sarcoma consists of sheets of uniform small round blue cells (often PAS-positive glycogen) with diffuse membranous CD99 and nuclear NKX2.2 positivity, confirmed by an EWSR1–FLI1 fusion. Malignant osteoid defines osteosarcoma.

items.q: The translocation t(11;22)(q24;q12) is diagnostic for which small round‑cell tumour?
items.e: t(11;22)(q24;q12) creates the EWSR1–FLI1 fusion found in about 85% of Ewing sarcomas. Desmoplastic small round cell tumour has a different translocation, t(11;22)(p13;q12), producing EWSR1–WT1.

items.q: The investigation of choice to localise the nidus of a suspected osteoid osteoma before radiofrequency ablation is:
items.e: Thin-section CT best shows the small lucent nidus (under 1.5–2 cm) with central mineralisation and surrounding sclerosis, and guides RFA. MRI shows extensive marrow and soft-tissue oedema that can obscure the nidus or mimic aggressive lesions.

items.q: In a meta‑analysis of 12 RCTs comparing minimally invasive total ankle replacement (MISTR) with open total ankle replacement (OTAR), heterogeneity was quantified as I² = 62 %. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: The results are homogeneous; pooling is justified.
There is considerable variability; a random‑effects model should be used.
The I² value indicates a high risk of bias in the studies.
Heterogeneity is too low to affect the overall estimate.
items.e: An I² of over 50 % reflects substantial heterogeneity; consequently, a random‑effects model is preferred to account for between‑study variation.

items.q: Which of the following statements about the GRADE system for evaluating evidence quality is false?
o: Randomized trials start as high‑quality evidence.
Observational studies begin as low‑quality evidence.
A large magnitude of effect can upgrade observational studies.
The presence of publication bias always downgrades evidence.
items.e: Publication bias is a consideration but does not automatically downgrade evidence; it is one of several factors assessed.

items.q: A patient with osteoarthritis of the knee undergoes a 12‑week supervised exercise program. The mean pain score before treatment is 6.5 (SD = 1.2); after treatment it is 4.8 (SD = 1.0). Assuming a paired t‑test was performed, the p‑value reported was 0.04. Which conclusion is most accurate?
o: The pain reduction is statistically significant, but without a control group it cannot be attributed to the exercise programme
The pain reduction is clinically significant but not statistically significant
The reduction is likely due to chance because p is close to 0.05
The exercise programme has been proven to cause the reduction in pain
items.e: p = 0.04 shows a statistically significant pre–post difference, but an uncontrolled before–after study cannot separate the effect of treatment from regression to the mean, natural history or placebo. A randomised control group is needed to infer causation.

items.q: In a prospective registry of 1,200 patients undergoing reverse shoulder arthroplasty, the 2‑year revision rate for glenoid loosening was 3.5 %. The 95 % confidence interval for the event rate was stated as 2.6 % to 4.6 %. What does this confidence interval represent?
o: The true revision rate in the population is exactly 3.5 %.
There is a 95 % chance that any future study will find a revision rate between 2.6 % and 4.6 %.
We can be 95 % confident that the population revision rate lies within 2.6 % to 4.6 %.
The interval reflects the variability between individual patient outcomes.
items.e: A 95 % confidence interval gives a range within which the true population parameter is expected to lie with 95 % confidence, based on the sample data.

items.q: A patient with active Paget disease of the pelvis and femur is scheduled for elective THA. Which preoperative measure is recommended to reduce intraoperative blood loss?
o: A course of bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronate) before surgery
items.e: Pagetic bone is hypervascular; antiresorptive treatment before elective surgery reduces disease activity (falling ALP) and vascularity, lowering blood loss. Teriparatide is contraindicated in Paget disease because of the osteosarcoma risk.

items.q: In a 45‑year‑old man with type 2 diabetes, serum calcium, phosphate and PTH are normal. He complains of diffuse bone pain. The investigation of choice to diagnose vitamin D‑deficiency osteomalacia is:
items.e: 25‑hydroxyvitamin D reflects body stores and is the screening test for vitamin D deficiency.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman on long-term oral glucocorticoids develops hip pain. The radiographic sign that indicates subchondral collapse in osteonecrosis of the femoral head is:
items.e: The crescent sign is a subchondral radiolucent line from collapse of necrotic subchondral bone (Ficat stage III, ARCO III). On MRI, the double-line sign on T2 is characteristic of osteonecrosis before collapse.

items.q: The most characteristic MRI finding in adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder is:
o: Thickening of the coracohumeral ligament with obliteration of the fat in the rotator interval
items.e: Frozen shoulder shows thickening of the coracohumeral ligament (over about 4 mm) and capsule, especially in the axillary recess, with loss of the subcoracoid fat triangle in the rotator interval. Joint volume is reduced rather than distended.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old footballer presents with a Bankart lesion and a glenoid bone defect measuring 12 mm (≈18% of the glenoid surface). What is the preferred surgical approach?
items.e: In a contact athlete, glenoid bone loss of about 18% exceeds the subcritical threshold (about 13.5%) above which Bankart repair has high failure rates. A bone-block procedure (Latarjet) restores the glenoid arc and adds the sling effect of the conjoint tendon.

items.q: A 4-year-old has a minimally displaced proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture treated in a long-leg cast. The parents should be warned about which late deformity?
items.e: The Cozen phenomenon is post-traumatic tibia valga after a proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture in young children, from asymmetric medial overgrowth. It peaks within about 1–2 years and usually resolves spontaneously, so early osteotomy is avoided.

items.q: A 15-month-old has a torus (buckle) fracture of the distal radius with under 10° angulation. The most appropriate management is:
o: Removable wrist splint for about 3 weeks without reduction
items.e: Torus fractures are stable compression injuries that heal and remodel reliably. A removable splint or soft bandage for about 3 weeks gives outcomes equal to casting (FORCE trial), and no reduction or routine follow-up radiographs are needed.

items.q: An 8-year-old boy weighing 28 kg has a closed, length-stable transverse mid-shaft femoral fracture. The preferred treatment is:
o: Skin traction followed by spica cast for 12 weeks
items.e: For children aged about 5–11 years with length-stable diaphyseal femoral fractures, ESIN (two titanium nails) is the standard (AAOS guideline). Spica casting suits children under 5, and submuscular plating or rigid lateral-entry nails are preferred for length-unstable fractures or weight over about 45–50 kg.

items.q: The most common organism in pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis of the finger is:
items.e: Staphylococcus aureus (increasingly MRSA) is the commonest cause. Pasteurella follows animal bites and Eikenella human bites. Kanavel signs are fusiform swelling, flexed resting posture, tenderness along the sheath and pain on passive extension.

items.q: All of the following statements about the Broström repair for chronic lateral ankle instability are TRUE EXCEPT:
o: It repairs the ATFL and CFL by imbrication
It is performed through a medial approach
The Gould modification reinforces it with the inferior extensor retinaculum
It is indicated after failure of 3–6 months of functional rehabilitation
items.e: The modified Broström–Gould is an anatomical lateral-ligament repair done through a lateral (anterolateral) incision: the attenuated ATFL and CFL are shortened and reattached to the fibula, then reinforced with the extensor retinaculum. Tendon-graft reconstruction is kept for poor tissue or failed repairs.

items.q: In the TNM staging of bone sarcomas, which of the following best describes the M component?
o: Presence of any regional lymph node metastases
Metabolic activity of the primary tumour on PET imaging
Evidence of distant organ or marrow spread at diagnosis
Involvement of the adjacent soft tissues beyond the cortex
items.e: M stands for ‘metastasis’ and is defined by the documented spread of tumour cells to distant organs or bone marrow at the time of diagnosis.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man with a known primary high‑grade osteosarcoma of the humerus undergoes whole‑body imaging. Which modality is preferred as the investigation of choice to detect pulmonary metastases?
items.e: Thin-section chest CT is the standard for detecting pulmonary metastases, the most common site of spread in osteosarcoma (about 15–20% at diagnosis). Bone scan or PET-CT is used to find skeletal metastases and skip lesions.

items.q: In the context of soft‑tissue sarcoma, the term ‘core needle biopsy’ is preferred over a ‘punch biopsy’ because:
o: It provides a larger tissue sample for histology and molecular studies
It is less invasive and avoids the need for general anaesthesia
It guarantees a negative margin with a single pass
It allows for immediate frozen section diagnosis during surgery
items.e: Core needle biopsy yields a larger, cylindric tissue core that is suitable for both routine histopathology and ancillary molecular testing, whereas a punch biopsy provides only a small, superficial specimen.

items.q: In the AJCC 8th edition staging of soft-tissue sarcoma of the trunk and extremities, a 12 cm primary tumour is classified as:
items.e: Since the AJCC 8th edition, T is based only on size: T1 up to 5 cm, T2 over 5 to 10 cm, T3 over 10 to 15 cm and T4 over 15 cm. The superficial/deep distinction was dropped, and grade (FNCLCC) remains part of the stage grouping.

items.q: Which molecule expressed by osteoblasts and osteocytes binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive their differentiation, and is the target of denosumab?
items.e: RANKL (with M-CSF) is required for osteoclastogenesis; osteoprotegerin is the natural decoy receptor that blocks it. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that mimics OPG.

items.q: Which component of the inorganic bone matrix is primarily responsible for endowing cortical bone with its ability to resist compressive forces?
items.e: Hydroxyapatite is the mineralized, calcium‑phosphate crystal that provides compressive strength; collagen gives tensile strength and osteocalcin and osteonectin act mainly as regulatory proteins.

items.q: During osteoclastic resorption, which cell type is chiefly responsible for secreting the proton pump that dissolves hydroxyapatite?
items.e: Osteoclasts secrete H⁺ via the vacuolar ATPase in the ruffled border, creating an acidic microenvironment that dissolves hydroxyapatite before collagen degradation.

items.q: Which factor, released from the bone matrix during osteoclastic resorption, recruits mesenchymal stem cells to the resorption site and so couples resorption with formation?
items.e: Latent TGF-β1 stored in bone matrix is activated by the acidic resorption environment and attracts osteoprogenitors to the resorption pit (Tang et al.); IGF-1 and osteoclast-derived factors such as ephrinB2 and S1P add to coupling. RANKL/OPG mainly regulates osteoclastogenesis, not coupling.

items.q: The most common monogenic disorder characterized by low bone density and frequent fractures in childhood is:
items.e: Osteogenesis imperfecta is an autosomal‑dominant collagen‑type I defect that results in brittle long bones and frequent fractures, making it the classic inherited bone fragility disorder.

items.q: A volar locking plate for a distal radius fracture is placed distal to the watershed line and left prominent. The tendon most at risk of attritional rupture is:
items.e: A plate that is prominent distal to the watershed line (Soong grade 2) abrades the FPL, which runs directly over the volar rim. EPL rupture after volar plating is usually caused by over-long dorsal screw tips.

items.q: A 62-year-old man has bilateral buttock and thigh pain on walking that is relieved by sitting and bending forward. Neurological examination is normal and MRI shows central canal stenosis at L4–L5 without spondylolisthesis. The most appropriate first-line management is:
o: Structured non-operative care: physiotherapy (flexion-based), analgesics and, if needed, epidural steroid injection
items.e: Neurogenic claudication without deficit is treated non-operatively first; about a third of patients improve and few deteriorate. Decompression (without fusion, as there is no instability) is offered if function remains limited, and fusion adds no benefit in stable stenosis (Försth, SLIP trials).

items.q: At revision THA for an aseptically loose femoral stem, the defect is classified as Paprosky type IIIA (non-supportive metaphysis, at least 4 cm of intact diaphyseal isthmus). An established reconstruction option is:
o: Extensively porous-coated cylindrical stem (or modular tapered fluted stem) engaging the isthmus
Cement-in-cement revision with a short polished stem
items.e: When the metaphysis cannot support fixation but at least 4 cm of isthmus remains (IIIA), distal diaphyseal fixation with an extensively porous-coated or tapered fluted stem is used. With under 4 cm of isthmus (IIIB), modular tapered stems are preferred, and type IV needs impaction grafting, an APC or a megaprosthesis.

items.q: A rugby player grabs an opponent's jersey and now cannot actively flex the DIP joint of his ring finger. The injury is:
o: Avulsion of flexor digitorum profundus from the distal phalanx
Volar plate avulsion of the PIP joint
items.e: Jersey finger is forced extension of an actively flexing DIP joint, avulsing FDP; the ring finger is involved in about 75% of cases. It is classified by Leddy–Packer according to the level of retraction, and type I (retracted into the palm) needs repair within about 7–10 days.

items.q: In the Bunnell opponensplasty for low median nerve palsy, the donor tendon is usually:
o: Flexor digitorum superficialis of the ring finger
items.e: Bunnell's transfer routes ring-finger FDS around a pulley at the pisiform (FCU loop) to the APB insertion. The alternatives are the Burkhalter (EIP), Camitz (palmaris longus, mainly abduction, used in severe carpal tunnel syndrome) and Huber (ADM, used in congenital thumb hypoplasia) transfers.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old marathon runner presents with a dull, aching pain 5 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion of the Achilles tendon, worse after running and relieved by over‑the‑counter NSAIDs. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic defect measuring 1.5 cm in length within the mid‑portion tendon. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Immediate surgical repair with tendon graft
Eccentric calf-loading exercise programme (Alfredson) with load modification
items.e: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy is a degenerative (tendinosis) condition; eccentric (or heavy slow resistance) loading for at least 12 weeks is first-line. Intratendinous steroid risks rupture, and surgery is kept for failure after 3–6 months.

items.q: The most common location for a spontaneous (atraumatic) rupture of the Achilles tendon occurs
o: Mid‑portion 2–6 cm proximal to the insertion
Tibial attachment of the proximal tendon
Near the musculotendinous junction 10 cm proximal to insertion
items.e: Spontaneous ruptures most frequently involve the mid‑portion 2–6 cm proximal to the insertion, where the tendon has the weakest micro‑architecture.

items.q: A 26-year-old basketball player jammed his middle finger 3 weeks ago. The PIP joint now rests in 30° flexion with DIP hyperextension. With the PIP flexed 90° over a table edge he cannot extend the middle phalanx and the DIP becomes rigid (positive Elson test). Which structure is ruptured?
o: Volar plate of the PIP joint
Central slip of the extensor mechanism
items.e: Central slip rupture causes a boutonnière deformity: the lateral bands sublux volar to the PIP axis, flexing the PIP and hyperextending the DIP. A rigid DIP during attempted PIP extension (Elson test) indicates central slip rupture.

items.q: A 55-year-old woman has a displaced distal radius fracture reduced and placed in a cast. Over the next 6 hours she develops progressively worsening numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers. The most appropriate management is:
o: Urgent carpal tunnel release with fracture stabilisation
Corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel
items.e: Progressive median nerve symptoms after a distal radius fracture indicate acute carpal tunnel syndrome, which needs urgent decompression and stabilisation of the fracture; stable, non-progressive symptoms after reduction can be observed.

items.q: Which nerve is most commonly affected acutely following a distal radius fracture?
o: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
items.e: Median nerve dysfunction (contusion or acute carpal tunnel syndrome) is the commonest neurological complication of distal radius fractures because the nerve lies directly volar to the fracture within the carpal tunnel.

items.q: In the Oberlin transfer for restoring elbow flexion after a C5–C6 brachial plexus injury, the ulnar nerve fascicle chosen as donor ideally supplies which muscle?
o: Flexor digitorum profundus to the little finger
items.e: Oberlin's technique transfers a redundant ulnar fascicle, preferably one predominantly supplying FCU (identified by stimulation), to the biceps motor branch of the musculocutaneous nerve, sparing intrinsic and grip function.

items.q: After a motorcycle accident a 45-year-old has complete sensory and motor loss in the ulnar nerve distribution with ipsilateral ptosis and miosis. Nerve conduction shows a normal ulnar sensory nerve action potential (SNAP). This combination indicates:
o: Postganglionic injury of the lower trunk
Preganglionic avulsion of the C8–T1 roots
Ulnar nerve laceration at the elbow
items.e: In preganglionic root avulsion the dorsal root ganglion cell bodies remain connected to their peripheral axons, so SNAPs are preserved in an anaesthetic territory; Horner syndrome further indicates T1 root avulsion.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a scaphoid waist non-union 9 months after injury. CT shows a humpback deformity with a lateral intrascaphoid angle of 50° and DISI; MRI shows a viable proximal pole. Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Volar approach with an interpositional corticocancellous wedge graft and screw fixation
Dorsal approach with a 1,2-ICSRA vascularised graft
items.e: A waist non-union with humpback deformity and a viable proximal pole is treated through a volar approach with an interpositional (Fisk–Fernandez) wedge graft to restore length and alignment; vascularised grafts are reserved for proximal pole avascular necrosis.

items.q: In the Herbert classification of scaphoid fractures, an acute, complete, unstable fracture of the scaphoid waist is classified as:
items.e: Herbert type A fractures are stable acute (A1 tubercle, A2 incomplete waist); type B are unstable acute: B1 distal oblique, B2 complete waist, B3 proximal pole, B4 trans-scaphoid perilunate, B5 comminuted.

items.q: A 2-year-old has radial polydactyly with two complete distal phalanges that both articulate with a single proximal phalanx. What is the Wassel type?
items.e: Wassel type II is a duplicated distal phalanx sharing one proximal phalanx; type I is a bifid distal phalanx, type III a bifid proximal phalanx and type IV (the commonest) a duplicated proximal phalanx.

items.q: Syndactyly of the border digits (thumb–index or ring–little) is released earlier, at about 6 months of age, than middle–ring syndactyly. The main reason is:
o: Unequal digit lengths cause progressive angular and rotational deformity of the longer digit
Border-digit syndactyly is always complex with bony fusion
Full-thickness skin grafts take better before 6 months
Web creep does not occur when release is done in infancy
items.e: Tethering of digits of unequal length (thumb–index, ring–little) causes progressive flexion, angular and rotational deformity, so these are released early; syndactyly between digits of similar length (middle–ring) is usually released at 12–18 months.

items.q: Which signalling centre in limb development, when duplicated, is responsible for ulnar dimelia (mirror hand)?
items.e: A second zone of polarising activity (sonic hedgehog source) on the preaxial side produces a mirror-image limb with a duplicated ulna, absent radius and no thumb (ulnar dimelia).

items.q: Synpolydactyly (fusion of the middle and ring fingers with a duplicated digit within the web) is caused by mutation of which gene?
items.e: Synpolydactyly is caused by HOXD13 mutations; HOXA13 causes hand-foot-genital syndrome, GLI3 causes Greig cephalopolysyndactyly and Pallister–Hall syndrome, and ZRS mutations cause preaxial polydactyly.

items.q: Which classification stages Dupuytren contracture for each ray by the total flexion deformity of the MCP, PIP and DIP joints, with the highest stage exceeding 135°?
items.e: Tubiana staging sums the flexion deformity of a ray: stage 1 0–45°, 2 45–90°, 3 90–135°, 4 over 135°. Luck described histological stages (proliferative, involutional, residual).

items.q: A 32-year-old woman has symptomatic hallux valgus with HVA 30°, IMA 12° and a distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA) of 18°; the first MTP joint is congruent. Which procedure corrects the deformity without making the joint incongruent?
o: Distal chevron osteotomy with lateral soft-tissue release
Biplanar (medial closing wedge) distal chevron osteotomy
items.e: A congruent joint with increased DMAA needs correction of the articular angle itself; the biplanar chevron removes a medial wedge to reorient the articular surface, whereas soft-tissue realignment would make the joint incongruent and risk stiffness or recurrence.

items.q: After a distal chevron osteotomy for hallux valgus, which uncorrected factor is most strongly associated with recurrence of the deformity?
o: An increased distal metatarsal articular angle
items.e: If an increased DMAA is left uncorrected, the laterally inclined articular surface drives the proximal phalanx back into valgus; capsular plication, stable fixation and an Akin osteotomy help prevent recurrence.

items.q: A 64-year-old active woman has severe hallux valgus (HVA 45°, IMA 18°) with painful arthritis of the first MTP joint on radiographs. Which procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: First MTP arthrodesis relieves pain from the arthritic joint and corrects severe deformity, and the IMA usually reduces after fusion; joint-preserving osteotomies do not treat arthritis, and Keller resection is reserved for low-demand elderly patients because of transfer metatarsalgia and cock-up toe.

items.q: After an Evans lateral column lengthening for a flexible adult flatfoot, a patient has persistent plantar-lateral foot pain under the cuboid and fifth metatarsal base. The most likely cause is:
items.e: Overlengthening the lateral column (too large a graft) stiffens the foot and overloads the lateral column, causing plantar-lateral pain; it is one of the commonest problems after lateral column lengthening.

items.q: A 74-year-old low-demand woman has posterior tibial tendon dysfunction with a flexible flatfoot: she cannot perform a single heel rise, but the hindfoot is passively correctable. The most appropriate initial treatment is:
o: Custom orthosis or ankle-foot orthosis with tendon-strengthening physiotherapy
Corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath
FDL transfer with medializing calcaneal osteotomy
items.e: Bracing (UCBL, AFO or Arizona brace) with tendon-strengthening exercises is first line, especially in low-demand elderly patients; steroid injection risks rupture, and surgery is for failure of non-operative care.

items.q: In a patient with a rigid adult flatfoot (fixed hindfoot valgus) and tibiotalar arthritis, the most suitable operative procedure is:
items.e: When the deformity is rigid and the ankle is arthritic, a tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) arthrodesis addresses both the hindfoot malalignment and the tibiotalar arthritis in one operation.

items.q: Which of the following statements about Achilles tendinopathy treatment is correct?
o: A large‑volume corticosteroid injection into the tendon is first‑line therapy
Eccentric loading is recommended for the mid‑portion subtype
ESWT is only indicated for insertional disease
Heavy‑weight resistance is contraindicated in the early phase
items.e: Eccentric loading (Alfredson protocol) is the established first‑line treatment for mid‑portion Achilles tendinopathy; corticosteroid injections are contraindicated as they can precipitate rupture.

items.q: A 45-year-old has 6 months of ankle pain and swelling, 4 years after a malleolar fracture. Which is the best initial investigation to assess post-traumatic ankle arthritis?
o: Weight-bearing AP, mortise and lateral radiographs of the ankle
items.e: Weight-bearing radiographs show true joint-space narrowing, alignment and malunion and are the first-line investigation; CT, SPECT-CT or MRI are adjuncts for planning.

items.q: In a displaced talar neck fracture, which vessel is considered most important to preserve because it may be the only remaining blood supply to the talar body?
o: Deltoid branch of the posterior tibial artery
Dorsalis pedis branches to the talar neck
items.e: The deltoid branch (from the artery of the tarsal canal) enters the medial talar body through the deltoid ligament and often survives displacement, so medial approaches and malleolar osteotomies must protect the deep deltoid ligament.

items.q: A snowboarder has a lateral process fracture of the talus. CT shows a single 1.5 cm fragment displaced 3 mm. The best treatment is:
items.e: Large lateral process fragments displaced more than 2 mm are treated by ORIF to restore the subtalar and talofibular articulations; small or comminuted fragments are excised and undisplaced fractures are casted.

items.q: Which statement about the Cedell fracture is correct?
o: It is an avulsion of the posterolateral tubercle of the posterior talar process
It is a fracture of the lateral process of the talus
It is a shearing osteochondral fracture of the talar dome
It is an avulsion of the posteromedial tubercle of the posterior talar process by the posterior tibiotalar ligament
items.e: A Cedell fracture is an avulsion of the posteromedial tubercle by the posterior tibiotalar ligament after dorsiflexion–pronation; the Shepherd fracture involves the posterolateral tubercle and the snowboarder's fracture the lateral process.

items.q: Intraoperatively, which fluoroscopic views are used to assess reduction of the posterior facet in a displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture?
items.e: Broden views (foot internally rotated about 40° with the beam angled 10–40° cephalad) profile the posterior facet from front to back; the Canale view shows the talar neck.

items.q: A Hawkins type I talar neck fracture, confirmed undisplaced on CT, is treated non-operatively. Standard management is:
o: Weight-bearing as tolerated in a boot from day one
Non-weight-bearing below-knee cast until union, usually 6–12 weeks
Full weight-bearing in a rigid cast for 12 weeks
Hinged brace with immediate ankle mobilisation
items.e: Undisplaced (Hawkins I) talar neck fractures are immobilised non-weight-bearing until radiological union; CT confirmation of no displacement is essential, and some surgeons use percutaneous screws to allow earlier motion.

items.q: A rugby player grabs an opponent's jersey and afterwards cannot actively flex the DIP joint of one finger. FDP avulsion (jersey finger) most commonly affects which finger?
items.e: About 75% of jersey finger injuries involve the ring finger, which is most prominent during grip and has a weaker FDP insertion; the Leddy–Packer classification is based on the level of tendon retraction.

items.q: A Zone II flexor tendon injury with a badly scarred sheath is reconstructed by first implanting a silicone rod to form a pseudosheath, followed by tendon grafting about 3 months later. This technique is attributed to:
items.e: Hunter's two-stage reconstruction uses a silicone rod to create a pseudosheath, then replaces it with a tendon graft such as palmaris longus; Kessler is a core suture, Kleinert a rehabilitation protocol, and Verdan described flexor zones.

items.q: A 50-year-old woman has nocturnal numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers, thenar wasting and weak thumb palmar abduction. Phalen test is positive. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Nocturnal symptoms, a positive Phalen test and abductor pollicis brevis weakness indicate median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel; pronator syndrome lacks night symptoms and affects palmar cutaneous sensation, and AIN syndrome is purely motor.

items.q: In which of the following is a Tinel sign expected to advance distally during recovery?
o: Unrepaired neurotmesis of the median nerve
Preganglionic avulsion of the C7 root
items.e: An advancing Tinel sign reflects regenerating axons growing down intact endoneurial tubes (axonotmesis); neurapraxia has no axonal regeneration, an unrepaired neurotmesis gives a static Tinel over a neuroma, and root avulsion does not regenerate.

items.q: A woman with rheumatoid arthritis suddenly loses active flexion of the thumb IP joint. Attrition rupture of flexor pollicis longus over a volar scaphoid osteophyte is known as:
items.e: The Mannerfelt–Norman lesion is FPL attrition rupture over a scaphoid or STT spur; the Vaughan-Jackson lesion is sequential rupture of EDM and ulnar EDC tendons over a prominent distal ulna.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old pharmacist presents with burning pain over the dorsoradial aspect of the hand triggered by forearm pronation. Electromyography shows no motor weakness. Which nerve is most likely compressed?
items.e: The described sensory distribution and lack of motor symptoms point to Wartenberg’s syndrome, compression of the superficial radial nerve.

items.q: After an anterior shoulder dislocation, a 25-year-old has weak shoulder abduction and external rotation with numbness over the lateral upper arm (regimental badge area). Which nerve is injured?
items.e: The axillary nerve (posterior cord, C5–C6) supplies deltoid, teres minor and the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm; a suprascapular nerve injury causes similar weakness without sensory loss.

items.q: A 30-year-old man has multiple brachial plexus root avulsions after a motorcycle crash and, 2 years later, severe burning deafferentation pain resistant to medication. Which surgical procedure is most effective for this pain?
o: Spinal accessory to suprascapular nerve transfer
items.e: DREZ lesioning ablates the hyperactive dorsal horn neurons responsible for deafferentation pain after root avulsion and relieves pain in most patients.

items.q: A 45-year-old has a flail arm after a fall and root avulsion is suspected. Which investigation is the traditional gold standard for showing pseudomeningoceles and absent rootlets?
o: CT myelography of the cervical spine
items.e: CT myelography shows pseudomeningoceles and absent ventral and dorsal rootlets, confirming preganglionic avulsion; MRI is increasingly used, while preserved SNAPs on NCS support but do not image the lesion.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a complete (pan-plexus) brachial plexus injury untreated for 18 months, with no elbow flexion. Which procedure is most appropriate for restoring elbow flexion?
o: Gracilis free functioning muscle transfer neurotised by the spinal accessory nerve
Biceps reinnervation by intercostal nerve transfer
items.e: After about 12–18 months the biceps motor end plates are lost, so a free functioning gracilis transfer driven by an extraplexal donor (spinal accessory or intercostals) is used; latissimus and Steindler transfers need muscles that are paralysed in a pan-plexus injury.

items.q: The normal range for the scapholunate angle on a lateral wrist radiograph is:
items.e: Normal scapholunate angles fall between 30–60° (mean ≈47°).

items.q: A 32-year-old construction worker has a tense, throbbing, swollen pulp of the index finger 3 days after a splinter injury, with the swelling confined to the distal phalanx. Which incision is preferred for drainage?
o: High mid-axial incision on the ulnar (non-contact) side
Transverse incision across the DIP flexion crease
Through-and-through incision dividing all pulp septa
items.e: A felon is drained through a high mid-axial incision on the non-contact side (ulnar for index to ring, radial for thumb and little finger), or a volar longitudinal incision if pointing; fish-mouth and through-and-through incisions destabilise the pulp and leave painful scars.

items.q: A 45-year-old diabetic has a painful swollen thenar eminence with the thumb held abducted and a widened first web space. The infection is confined to the thenar space. Which approach provides adequate drainage?
o: Volar incision along the thenar crease combined with a dorsal longitudinal incision in the first web
Single volar longitudinal incision from the wrist to the thumb tip
Transverse incision across the first web commissure
Mid-axial incision along the radial border of the thumb
items.e: The thenar space lies volar to adductor pollicis and deep to the index flexor tendons; it is drained by a thenar crease incision (protecting the motor branch of the median nerve) plus a dorsal first-web incision, avoiding a transverse commissure incision that causes web contracture.

items.q: A 27-year-old dental hygienist has throbbing pain at the tip of the index finger with clustered clear vesicles on an erythematous base; the pulp is not tense. Which statement best guides management?
o: Unroof and drain the vesicles to prevent spread
Use a protective dressing, with oral aciclovir if seen early
Drain through a mid-axial incision as for a felon
items.e: Herpetic whitlow is self-limiting HSV infection; incision risks secondary bacterial infection and viral spread, so it is managed with a protective dressing and early oral antivirals.

items.q: A 50-year-old diabetic presents 3 days after a puncture wound with a fusiform swollen ring finger held in flexion, tenderness along the flexor sheath and severe pain on passive extension. The most appropriate management is:
o: Intravenous antibiotics and splinting with review at 48 hours
Urgent surgical drainage with flexor sheath irrigation plus intravenous antibiotics
Corticosteroid injection into the flexor sheath
items.e: All four Kanavel signs in a diabetic with established infection indicate pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis needing urgent drainage and sheath irrigation (proximal A1 and distal incisions) with IV antibiotics; a trial of antibiotics alone is only for very early cases seen within about 24–48 hours.

items.q: Which organism is least likely to be the culprit in a community‑acquired hand infection following a simple finger prick?
items.e: Community‑acquired hand infections usually involve S. aureus (often MRSA), beta‑haemolytic streptococci, or mixed anaerobes in bites. Mycobacterium marinum is associated with chronic fish‑tank related infections, not a simple prick.

items.q: Which is the most common late complication after surgical release of syndactyly?
items.e: Web creep, the distal migration of the reconstructed commissure, is the commonest late complication, especially with graft loss, early release or inadequate commissural flaps, and often needs revision.

items.q: Isolated postaxial polydactyly of the hand, often inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, is most common in which population?
items.e: Isolated postaxial (ulnar) polydactyly is about ten times more common in people of African descent and is usually autosomal dominant; in other populations it is more often syndromic and should prompt evaluation.

items.q: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis suddenly cannot extend her little finger. There is a tender, prominent distal ulna. Which tendon is most likely ruptured first?
o: Extensor digitorum communis to the ring finger
Flexor digitorum profundus of the little finger
items.e: In the Vaughan-Jackson lesion, attrition over the eroded, dorsally prominent distal ulna ruptures the most ulnar extensor first, the extensor digiti minimi, then the EDC tendons from ulnar to radial.

items.q: After a proximal crescentic osteotomy of the first metatarsal for severe hallux valgus, which complication is most frequently reported?
o: Avascular necrosis of the metatarsal head
items.e: Proximal crescentic osteotomies are inherently unstable in the sagittal plane and commonly heal in dorsiflexion, unloading the first ray and causing transfer metatarsalgia under the lesser metatarsal heads.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old obese woman presents with medial ankle pain that worsens when she attempts a single‑leg heel‑rise; the heel does not invert. Which tendon is most likely dysfunctional?
items.e: Impaired inversion on heel rise is the classic sensitive test for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, the main dynamic stabiliser of the medial arch.

items.q: On a weight-bearing lateral foot radiograph, the talus–first metatarsal (Meary) angle is 12° with the apex pointing plantarward. This indicates:
items.e: Meary's angle is normally about 0° (±4°); a plantar apex indicates planus (about 4–15° mild, 15–30° moderate, over 30° severe), while a dorsal apex indicates cavus.

items.q: In middle-aged obese women, which is the most common initiating lesion of adult acquired flatfoot deformity?
items.e: Degeneration of the tibialis posterior tendon is the usual initiating event; the spring ligament, talocalcaneal interosseous and later deltoid ligaments fail secondarily as the deformity progresses.

items.q: Which investigation is the investigation of choice for detecting tears or tendinosis of the tibialis posterior tendon in suspected adult acquired flatfoot?
items.e: MRI provides direct visualization of tendon integrity, flow voids, and inflammatory changes, making it the gold standard for TP tendon assessment.

items.q: A 48-year-old has a neglected Achilles rupture of 3 months' duration with a 4 cm gap after debridement of the tendon ends. Which reconstruction is most appropriate?
o: V-Y lengthening of the gastrocnemius aponeurosis with or without FHL transfer
Tenodesis of the FDL to the calcaneus
items.e: In the Myerson scheme, defects of about 2–5 cm are bridged by V-Y advancement of the gastrocnemius aponeurosis, often augmented with an FHL transfer; small defects allow end-to-end repair and defects over 5 cm need FHL transfer with or without grafting.

items.q: During assessment of an infected diabetic foot ulcer, the probe-to-bone test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: A positive probe-to-bone test has a high positive predictive value for osteomyelitis in infected ulcers (high-prevalence settings); confirmation is with imaging and bone biopsy.

items.q: A diabetic patient with a plantar forefoot ulcer has an ABI of 1.35 but TcPO₂ at the dorsum of the toe measures 25 mmHg. What does this suggest?
o: Peripheral arterial disease is adequately managed
The ABI is falsely high due to medial calcification
The toe has adequate perfusion for healing
items.e: A high ABI (>1.3) can be falsely reassuring because of calcification; low toe pressure or TcPO₂ indicates true ischemia that would impair healing.

items.q: What is the gold-standard offloading method for an uncomplicated, non-infected neuropathic plantar forefoot ulcer in a patient without significant ischaemia?
items.e: A non-removable total contact cast (or a removable walker made non-removable) is the gold standard because it enforces compliance and redistributes plantar pressure; it is avoided when infection or severe ischaemia is present.

items.q: What is the most common cause of ankle arthritis?
items.e: About 70–80% of ankle arthritis is post-traumatic (after malleolar or pilon fractures and recurrent instability), unlike hip and knee arthritis, which is mostly primary.

items.q: After a modified Broström–Gould repair for chronic lateral ankle instability, which nerve is most frequently injured?
items.e: The intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve crosses the anterolateral ankle near the incision and is the nerve most commonly injured after Broström-type repairs.

items.q: A 26-year-old has recurrent giving way of the ankle after several inversion sprains. What is the first-line management of chronic lateral ankle instability?
o: Supervised neuromuscular and proprioceptive training with peroneal strengthening for at least 3 months
items.e: Functional rehabilitation (balance, proprioceptive and peroneal strengthening) with bracing is first line; surgery such as the Broström–Gould repair is considered when mechanical instability persists after adequate rehabilitation.

items.q: Which is the main indication for surgical stabilisation in chronic lateral ankle instability?
o: Persistent mechanical instability despite 3–6 months of supervised rehabilitation
A single acute grade II sprain
Functional giving way with normal stress tests that improves with physiotherapy
items.e: Surgery is indicated for recurrent instability that persists after adequate functional rehabilitation, usually with mechanical laxity on stress testing; generalised laxity is a reason to augment the repair rather than an indication itself.

items.q: Which imaging modality is essential to confirm a suspected talar neck fracture and to assess comminution?
items.e: CT provides detailed bone anatomy and reveals displacement and comminution that plain radiographs may miss.

items.q: During open reduction of a talar neck fracture, which surgical approach is preferred to allow accurate assessment of reduction while preserving the deltoid ligament?
items.e: A dual anteromedial + anterolateral approach gives complementary views of the neck and avoids compromising the deltoid ligament that supplies the medial body.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a bony mallet finger involving 45% of the articular surface with volar subluxation of the distal phalanx. The most appropriate treatment is:
o: Stack splint for 2 weeks then mobilisation
Closed reduction and extension-block K-wire pinning
items.e: Bony mallet injuries with volar subluxation of the distal phalanx (often with more than a third of the joint involved) are treated surgically, commonly by extension-block pinning (Ishiguro); most other mallet injuries do well with continuous extension splinting.

items.q: A boxer has painful snapping of the extensor tendon into the ulnar gutter of the middle finger MCP joint when making a fist. Which structure is most likely torn?
o: Radial sagittal band of the middle finger
Ulnar sagittal band of the middle finger
Juncturae tendinum between middle and ring fingers
Central slip of the middle finger
items.e: Boxer's knuckle most often involves rupture of the radial sagittal band of the middle finger, allowing the EDC tendon to subluxate ulnarward during MCP flexion.

items.q: After repair of a ring finger FDP laceration with excessive tendon advancement, the patient cannot fully flex the adjacent middle and little fingers. This phenomenon is called:
items.e: The FDP tendons of the ulnar three fingers share a common muscle belly, so shortening one tendon prevents the others from reaching full excursion (quadriga effect).

items.q: After an FDP laceration distal to the lumbrical origin, a patient's PIP joint paradoxically extends when he tries to flex the finger. This is known as:
items.e: When FDP is divided distal to the lumbrical origin (or a graft is too long), FDP pull is transmitted through the lumbrical to the lateral bands, extending the IP joints on attempted flexion (lumbrical plus).

items.q: For a Zone II flexor tendon repair intended to allow early active motion, what is the minimum number of core suture strands generally recommended?
items.e: Repair strength is roughly proportional to the number of core strands crossing the repair; at least a four-strand core repair with an epitendinous suture is recommended for early active motion protocols.

items.q: A patient with cubital tunnel syndrome flexes the thumb IP joint when asked to grip a sheet of paper between the thumb and index finger (Froment sign). Weakness of which muscle is being compensated?
items.e: Froment sign reflects weakness of adductor pollicis (ulnar nerve), compensated by the median-innervated flexor pollicis longus, which flexes the thumb IP joint.

items.q: A ganglion in Guyon's canal causes wasting of the interossei with normal sensation in the little finger. In which zone of Guyon's canal is the lesion?
items.e: Zone I (proximal to the bifurcation) gives mixed motor and sensory loss, zone II surrounds the deep motor branch (pure motor deficit) and zone III surrounds the superficial sensory branch (pure sensory deficit).

items.q: A patient has finger and thumb drop with radial deviation on wrist extension but normal sensation. What is the most common site of posterior interosseous nerve compression?
o: Fibrous bands anterior to the radiocapitellar joint
Proximal edge of the supinator (arcade of Frohse)
items.e: The arcade of Frohse, the fibrous proximal edge of the superficial supinator, is the commonest site of PIN compression; radial deviation occurs because ECRL (supplied proximal to the PIN) is spared while ECU is weak.

items.q: In the Sunderland classification of nerve injury, an injury in which the axons, endoneurium and perineurium are disrupted but the epineurium is intact is grade:
items.e: Sunderland I is neurapraxia, II axonotmesis, III adds endoneurial disruption, IV adds perineurial disruption with only the epineurium intact (neuroma-in-continuity, usually needs surgery), and V is complete transection.

items.q: In suspected anterior interosseous nerve syndrome, how is pronator quadratus tested in isolation?
o: Resisted pronation with the elbow fully flexed
Resisted pronation with the elbow fully extended
Resisted supination with the elbow flexed
items.e: Full elbow flexion slackens the humeral head of pronator teres, so resisted pronation in this position tests pronator quadratus, which is supplied by the AIN.

items.q: A newborn after a difficult delivery has a flail, insensate arm with ipsilateral ptosis and miosis. What is the Narakas group?
items.e: Narakas group I is C5–C6, II is C5–C7, III is a flail arm (C5–T1) and IV is a flail arm with Horner syndrome, which carries the worst prognosis.

items.q: According to Gilbert and Tassin, the classic indication for primary brachial plexus exploration in obstetric brachial plexus palsy is absence of biceps recovery by what age?
items.e: Absent biceps function at 3 months predicts poor spontaneous recovery and was Gilbert and Tassin's indication for microsurgery; others use the Toronto test score or the cookie test at 9 months.

items.q: In an adult with a traumatic brachial plexus injury, an elevated hemidiaphragm on chest radiograph suggests:
o: Proximal injury at the C5 root level
items.e: The phrenic nerve receives a C5 contribution near the roots, so diaphragmatic paralysis indicates a very proximal (root-level) injury of the upper plexus and a poorer prognosis for spontaneous recovery.

items.q: A lateral wrist radiograph after a fall shows the lunate tipped volarly out of the lunate fossa while the capitate remains aligned with the radius. Which Mayfield stage of progressive perilunar instability is this?
items.e: Mayfield stages progress from scapholunate disruption (I) to capitolunate (II) and lunotriquetral (III) disruption, ending with lunate dislocation from the radius (IV) after failure of the dorsal radiocarpal ligaments.

items.q: The Reagan ballottement (shuck) test is used to assess instability of which ligament?
items.e: In the Reagan test the lunate is stabilised while the triquetrum is shifted dorsally and volarly; pain or excessive laxity suggests lunotriquetral ligament injury, which can lead to VISI.

items.q: A 28-year-old has Lichtman stage II Kienböck disease with 2 mm negative ulnar variance. Which procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: In early Kienböck disease (stages I–IIIA) with ulnar-negative variance, joint-levelling by radial shortening unloads the lunate; salvage procedures are for stage IIIB and IV.

items.q: A 60-year-old has SLAC wrist with arthritis at the radioscaphoid and capitolunate joints, and a preserved radiolunate joint. Which procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: In SLAC stage III the capitolunate joint is arthritic, which contraindicates proximal row carpectomy; scaphoid excision with four-corner fusion uses the spared radiolunate articulation.

items.q: Two days after punching someone in the mouth, a man has an infected wound over the third MCP joint. Which organism, characteristic of human bites, must be covered by antibiotics?
items.e: Eikenella corrodens, a human oral commensal, is characteristic of fight bites; treatment is surgical exploration and washout of the MCP joint with amoxicillin-clavulanate. Pasteurella is typical of cat and dog bites.

items.q: A dishwasher has a chronic paronychia with nail-fold thickening and loss of the cuticle for several months. The most commonly implicated organism is:
items.e: Chronic paronychia in people whose hands are repeatedly wet is usually due to Candida albicans; it is treated by keeping hands dry, topical antifungals or steroids, and eponychial marsupialisation if refractory.

items.q: Infection of the thumb flexor sheath spreads to the little finger sheath, producing a horseshoe abscess. Through which space do the radial and ulnar bursae communicate?
items.e: The radial bursa (FPL sheath) and ulnar bursa (little finger sheath) can communicate through Parona's space, deep in the distal forearm between pronator quadratus and the flexor tendons.

items.q: In the Bayne and Klug classification of radial longitudinal deficiency, which type is the most common?
items.e: Complete absence of the radius (type IV) is the commonest form and causes marked radial deviation of the hand, usually treated by centralisation or radialisation after soft-tissue stretching.

items.q: An infant has bilateral absent radii, but both thumbs are present. The associated condition is most likely:
items.e: TAR syndrome characteristically spares the thumbs despite absent radii; in Holt–Oram, Fanconi anaemia and VACTERL the thumb is usually hypoplastic or absent.

items.q: A child with radial longitudinal deficiency has a normal blood count. Which test should be done before surgery to exclude Fanconi anaemia?
items.e: Bone marrow failure in Fanconi anaemia usually appears around 5–10 years of age, so a chromosomal breakage test (DEB or mitomycin C) is needed in all children with radial deficiency, even with a normal blood count.

items.q: A 1-year-old has Blauth type IIIB thumb hypoplasia with an unstable carpometacarpal joint. The recommended treatment is:
items.e: Blauth types IIIB, IV and V lack a stable CMC joint, so the thumb cannot be reconstructed and index pollicisation is advised; types II and IIIA with a stable CMC are reconstructed.

items.q: A child has complex syndactyly of all fingers (mitten hand) with craniosynostosis. The gene most commonly mutated is:
items.e: Apert syndrome (acrocephalosyndactyly) is caused by FGFR2 gain-of-function mutations; FGFR3 causes achondroplasia and HOXD13 causes synpolydactyly.

items.q: In Dupuytren disease causing PIP contracture, which cord displaces the digital neurovascular bundle superficially and toward the midline, putting it at risk during fasciectomy?
items.e: The spiral cord is formed from the pretendinous band, spiral band, lateral digital sheet and Grayson ligament; it wraps around the neurovascular bundle and displaces it centrally and superficially.

items.q: Which feature is part of the Dupuytren diathesis that predicts aggressive disease and recurrence?
items.e: Dupuytren diathesis includes early onset (under 50), male sex, family history, bilateral disease and ectopic lesions such as Garrod knuckle pads, Ledderhose and Peyronie disease.

items.q: The most common thumb deformity in rheumatoid arthritis, with MCP flexion and IP hyperextension, is which Nalebuff type?
items.e: Nalebuff type I (boutonnière thumb) is the commonest and starts with MCP synovitis attenuating the EPB and dorsal capsule; type III is the swan-neck thumb from CMC disease.

items.q: A 45-year-old has pain at the end of dorsiflexion of the hallux with a dorsal first metatarsal head osteophyte and well-preserved joint space (early hallux rigidus). The procedure of choice is:
o: Hemiarthroplasty of the first MTP joint
items.e: Cheilectomy, removing the dorsal osteophyte and about a quarter to a third of the dorsal head, relieves dorsal impingement in early grades; arthrodesis is preferred for advanced arthritis with pain in mid-range motion.

items.q: In Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, the plantarflexed first ray of the cavovarus foot results from which muscle imbalance?
items.e: A relatively strong peroneus longus overpowers a weak tibialis anterior, plantarflexing the first ray; a strong tibialis posterior against a weak peroneus brevis drives hindfoot varus.

items.q: A 14-year-old with recurrent ankle sprains has a rigid flatfoot. The lateral radiograph shows a continuous C-shaped line formed by the medial talar dome and the sustentaculum tali. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: The C sign indicates a talocalcaneal coalition, typically of the middle facet, best confirmed on CT; the anteater sign is typical of a calcaneonavicular coalition.

items.q: A skier has painful snapping behind the lateral malleolus. The ankle radiograph shows a small cortical flake avulsed from the lateral rim of the distal fibula (fleck sign). This indicates:
o: Avulsion of the superior peroneal retinaculum with peroneal tendon dislocation
items.e: The fleck sign is a cortical rim avulsion at the superior peroneal retinaculum insertion (Eckert–Davis grade III) and indicates peroneal tendon subluxation or dislocation, which usually requires surgical repair.

items.q: In the Brodsky anatomical classification of Charcot neuroarthropathy of the foot, which region is most commonly involved?
items.e: Brodsky type 1, the midfoot (tarsometatarsal and naviculocuneiform joints), accounts for most cases and often leads to a rocker-bottom deformity with plantar ulceration.

items.q: A diabetic has a deep plantar ulcer with an underlying abscess and osteomyelitis, without gangrene. What is the Wagner grade?
items.e: Wagner grade 1 is a superficial ulcer, grade 2 a deep ulcer to tendon or capsule, grade 3 a deep ulcer with abscess or osteomyelitis, grade 4 forefoot gangrene and grade 5 whole-foot gangrene.

items.q: What is the recommended position for ankle arthrodesis?
o: 10° plantarflexion, neutral hindfoot and neutral rotation
10° dorsiflexion, 10° hindfoot varus and internal rotation
Neutral dorsiflexion, 10° hindfoot varus and 15° external rotation
Neutral dorsiflexion, about 5° hindfoot valgus, external rotation matching the other side, with the talus slightly posterior
items.e: Neutral flexion with slight valgus and external rotation (about 5–10°, like the opposite side) and posterior talar translation reduces stress on adjacent joints and improves gait; plantarflexion causes knee hyperextension (back-knee thrust).

items.q: A 58-year-old diabetic with end-stage ankle destruction asks about total ankle replacement. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to total ankle arthroplasty?
items.e: Charcot neuroarthropathy, active infection, severe peripheral vascular disease and extensive talar avascular necrosis are absolute contraindications; inflammatory arthritis and bilateral disease are common indications.

items.q: A 50-year-old has asymmetric varus ankle arthritis with medial joint-space narrowing and a preserved lateral half of the tibiotalar joint. Which joint-preserving procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: A medial opening-wedge supramalleolar osteotomy corrects the varus tibial plafond and shifts load to the preserved lateral joint; it suits asymmetric arthritis with at least half the joint preserved.

items.q: The Sanders classification of intra-articular calcaneal fractures is based on:
o: Böhler angle on the lateral radiograph
Harris axial view showing heel widening
Number of posterior facet fragments on coronal CT at its widest point
Involvement of the calcaneocuboid joint on axial CT
items.e: Sanders types I–IV are defined by the number and position of fracture lines through the posterior facet on the coronal CT slice showing the widest undersurface of the facet; type IV (comminuted) has the worst prognosis.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a displaced tongue-type calcaneal fracture; the posterior heel skin is blanched and tented over the tuberosity fragment. The most appropriate management is:
o: Elevation and delayed ORIF at 10–14 days
Delayed fixation once the wrinkle test is positive
Urgent reduction and fixation of the tuberosity fragment
items.e: Posterior skin tenting from a displaced tongue-type or tuberosity fragment is a surgical emergency, because pressure necrosis of the heel skin develops within hours; the fragment is reduced and fixed urgently, often percutaneously.

items.q: The full-thickness flap of the extensile lateral approach to the calcaneus depends mainly on which artery?
o: Lateral calcaneal artery (branch of the peroneal artery)
items.e: The lateral calcaneal artery runs within the flap close to the vertical limb of the incision; injury to it contributes to the wound-edge necrosis that has made sinus tarsi and percutaneous approaches more popular.

items.q: During posterior ankle arthroscopy for os trigonum excision, which structure marks the medial limit of safe working because the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle lies just medial to it?
items.e: The FHL tendon runs between the medial and lateral tubercles of the posterior talar process; staying lateral to it protects the tibial nerve and posterior tibial vessels.

items.q: A 24-year-old rugby player presents with an inability to actively flex the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint of his ring finger after a tackling injury. Active flexion at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and metacarpophalangeal joints is fully preserved. Which tendon has been avulsed?
items.e: Jersey finger is an avulsion of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon at the base of the distal phalanx (Zone I), most commonly affecting the ring finger during forced extension while actively flexing. Because the FDS remains intact, active PIP joint flexion is preserved while isolated DIP joint flexion is lost.

items.q: A 35-year-old amateur boxer presents with persistent painful ulnar subluxation of the extensor digitorum communis tendon of the middle finger and an active MCP joint extension lag after 8 weeks of failed splinting. Which operative intervention is indicated?
o: Extensor tendon centralisation and sagittal band reconstruction
Lateral band mobilisation and triangular ligament reconstruction
Extensor indicis proprius to extensor digitorum communis transfer
items.e: Chronic symptomatic sagittal band rupture ('boxer's knuckle', Zone V) refractory to conservative splinting is managed with extensor tendon centralisation and sagittal band reconstruction (often using a slip of EDC or junctura tendinum). Lateral band procedures and Fowler tenotomy address PIP/DIP pathomechanics (boutonniere or mallet), not sagittal band subluxation at the MCP joint.

items.q: A 22-year-old athlete sustains a closed mallet finger injury of the little finger with an avulsion fracture involving less than 20% of the articular surface and no joint subluxation. What is the standard initial management?
o: Continuous DIP joint extension splinting for 6 to 8 weeks with the PIP joint left free
Immobilisation of both DIP and PIP joints in neutral extension for 4 weeks
Closed reduction and percutaneous extension-block pinning (Ishiguro technique)
Open reduction and internal fixation with a mini-fragment screw
items.e: Closed mallet finger injuries with small bony fragments (<20-30% of the articular surface) without volar subluxation are managed conservatively with continuous DIP joint extension splinting for 6-8 weeks, leaving the PIP joint completely free. Extension-block pinning or ORIF is indicated when there is volar subluxation of the distal phalanx or a large fragment (>30-50% articular surface).

items.q: During repair of flexor tendons in Zone II of the finger, which annular pulleys are biomechanically the most critical to preserve in order to prevent bowstringing and loss of tendon excursion?
items.e: The A2 pulley (over the proximal phalanx) and A4 pulley (over the middle phalanx) are biomechanically the most vital to preserve to prevent bowstringing. The A1, A3, and A5 pulleys overlie the MCP, PIP, and DIP joints respectively and can be vented or divided without significant biomechanical compromise.

items.q: Which of the following technical factors has the greatest positive correlation with the ultimate tensile strength of a primary flexor tendon repair in Zone II?
o: The number of core suture strands crossing the repair site
Placing the core suture purchase within 2 mm of the lacerated tendon ends
Locating the core suture predominantly along the volar half of the tendon
Omitting the running epitendinous suture to prevent repair bulk
items.e: Primary repair tensile strength is directly proportional to the number of core suture strands crossing the repair site (4- to 6-strand repairs allow early active motion). Suture purchase should be 7-10 mm from the cut end (2 mm cuts through easily), sutures placed dorsally provide superior strength, and an epitendinous suture adds 10-50% to repair strength.

items.q: A patient with an undisplaced waist scaphoid fracture is managed with a below‑elbow cast for how many weeks to achieve >90% union?
items.e: Undisplaced waist fractures require 6–8 weeks of below‑elbow immobilisation for optimal union.

items.q: Which ligament provides the strongest intrinsic restraint to lunotriquetral instability?
items.e: The palmar portion of the lunotriquetral ligament is the most robust stabiliser against lunotriquetral dissociation.

items.q: A 30‑year‑old tennis player has a displaced waist scaphoid fracture (> 2 mm). What is the most appropriate initial surgical approach?
o: Open reduction and internal fixation with a headless compression screw via a volar approach
Open reduction with dorsal approach fixation
Closed reduction and long arm cast
items.e: Displaced waist fractures (> 1–2 mm) are best managed by ORIF with a volar headless screw, preserving the dorsal blood supply.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old patient presents with a firm, tense swelling over the first web space that is non‑tender to palpation but painful on thumb opposition. The swelling is not contiguous with the dorsal hand. What space is most likely involved?
items.e: Pain on thumb opposition and swelling of the first web space are characteristic of a thenar space abscess.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old woman presents with a painful hallux valgus, an HVA of 32° and an IMA of 14°. The first TMT joint is clinically lax and the DMAA is 12°. Which surgical procedure corrects the deformity and stabilises the first TMT joint?
o: Scarf osteotomy followed by Akin osteotomy
items.e: The deformity is moderate with a hypermobile first TMT joint; a modified Lapidus fuses the first TMT joint and corrects the IMA simultaneously.

items.q: During a chevron osteotomy for hallux valgus, the surgeon performs an extensive medial capsulotomy and releases the adductor hallucis. Which complication is most likely if the lateral soft‑tissue constraints are not adequately addressed?
o: Avascular necrosis of the first metatarsal head
Neuroma of the medial dorsal cutaneous nerve
items.e: Excessive medial release without balancing lateral structures tips the hallux into varus (inverse of the intended valgus correction).

items.q: A 45‑year‑old obese woman presents with progressive medial ankle pain that worsens during stair climbing. On examination she cannot invert her foot during a single‑limb heel‑rise test. Which structure is most likely dysfunctional?
items.e: The inability to invert the foot on heel rise is the most sensitive test for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, the primary dynamic stabiliser of the medial arch.

items.q: During a medialising displacement calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO) for flexible flatfoot, which neurovascular structure is most at risk?
o: Surrounding the lateral wall of the 5th metatarsal
The medial calcaneal branch of the posterior tibial artery
The sural nerve and lateral calcaneal branch
items.e: The medial side of the calcaneal osteotomy is close to the sural nerve and its lateral branch; these are most at risk when shifting the calcaneus medially.

items.q: The hypovascular watershed zone of the Achilles tendon lies what distance proximal to its calcaneal insertion?
items.e: The watershed zone is classically described as 2–6 cm above the insertion where most ruptures occur.

items.q: After flexor tendon surgery a patient cannot fully flex the uninjured fingers of the same hand and has a weak grip (quadriga effect). Which technical error most commonly produces this?
o: Excision of one slip of FDS in zone II
Excessive advancement or shortening of a single FDP tendon
Repair of the lumbrical origin under tension
items.e: The FDP tendons of the ulnar three fingers share a common muscle belly, so shortening or over-advancing one FDP (e.g. >1 cm, or tenodesing it to an extensor) limits excursion of the others, producing the quadriga effect.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a closed injury to the dorsum of the PIP joint of the middle finger. Which test is most reliable for diagnosing an acute central slip rupture before a boutonnière deformity develops?
items.e: In the Elson test the PIP is flexed 90° over a table edge and the patient extends the middle phalanx against resistance; with a ruptured central slip the force passes through the lateral bands and the DIP becomes rigidly extended.

items.q: A 58-year-old diabetic with loss of protective sensation has a plantar ulcer under the great toe; probe-to-bone is positive but plain radiographs are normal. Which imaging is most appropriate to confirm osteomyelitis?
items.e: MRI is the preferred advanced imaging for diabetic foot osteomyelitis (IWGDF/IDSA); radiographs lag 2–3 weeks and a three-phase bone scan is sensitive but non-specific in the neuropathic foot.

items.q: Which component of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis contributes the greatest share of syndesmotic stability?
o: Posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (with transverse ligament)
Interosseous membrane 5 cm above the plafond
items.e: In Ogilvie-Harris's sectioning study the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament complex provided about 42% of syndesmotic stability, the AITFL about 35% and the interosseous ligament about 22%.

items.q: A dental hygienist has a painful fingertip with clusters of clear vesicles on an erythematous base; the pulp is not tense. Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Incision and drainage of the vesicles
Protective dressing ± oral acyclovir; avoid incision
items.e: This is herpetic whitlow (HSV); it is self-limiting, and incision is contraindicated because it risks secondary bacterial infection and viral spread, so treatment is supportive with antivirals if early.

items.q: An infant has a Wassel IV thumb duplication. At what age is surgical reconstruction (excision of the hypoplastic radial thumb with collateral ligament and APB reconstruction) usually performed?
items.e: Reconstruction is usually done around 1 year of age, when anaesthesia is safer and structures are larger, but before pinch and cortical hand patterns develop.

items.q: Which molecule secreted by the apical ectodermal ridge directs proximodistal outgrowth of the developing limb?
items.e: The AER controls proximodistal growth via FGFs (FGF8, FGF4); SHH from the ZPA controls radioulnar patterning, and WNT7a/LMX1B control dorsoventral patterning.

items.q: Which of the following does NOT indicate an unstable (displaced) scaphoid waist fracture?
o: Fracture step or gap > 1 mm on CT
items.e: Instability criteria include displacement >1 mm, intrascaphoid angle >35°, height-to-length ratio >0.65, radiolunate angle >15° and scapholunate angle >60°; a scapholunate angle of 50° lies within the normal 30–60° range.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old electrician presents with a pustular, erythematous lesion over the lateral nail fold of the right index finger that has spread to the surrounding skin within 24 hours. There is no history of trauma, but he reports frequent nail biting. Which organism is most likely responsible?
items.e: Acute paronychia from nail biting is classically due to S. aureus.

items.q: A 32‑year‑old man with type 2 diabetes develops a painful, fluctuating swelling over the volar surface of the distal phalanx of the thumb after a minor prick. Warm‑soaked pads are ineffective. What is the first step in management?
o: Incise and drain the pulpal abscess
items.e: Pulpal (felon) abscess requires prompt incision and drainage; earlier antibiotics alone are inadequate.

items.q: A footballer feels sudden pain in the posterior heel during a sprint; the Thompson (calf squeeze) test shows no plantarflexion. Which of the following is a recognised risk factor for this injury?
items.e: Fluoroquinolones (especially with corticosteroids and age >60) increase the risk of Achilles tendinopathy and rupture through effects on tenocyte matrix metabolism.

items.q: On an anterior drawer stress radiograph of the ankle, which absolute anterior talar translation indicates ATFL insufficiency?
items.e: Absolute anterior translation >10 mm, or >3 mm more than the opposite side, indicates ATFL insufficiency; talar tilt >10° (or >5° side-to-side) indicates added CFL insufficiency.

items.q: A patient has chronic lateral ankle instability with a hindfoot-driven cavovarus foot. Which additional procedure most reduces the risk of failure of a Broström repair?
items.e: Hindfoot varus overloads the lateral ligaments; a lateralising (Dwyer-type) calcaneal osteotomy corrects it, with a first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy added if the deformity is forefoot-driven.

items.q: A fracture of the medial tubercle of the posterior process of the talus (Cedell fracture) is usually an avulsion caused by which structure?
o: Posterior tibiotalar part of the deltoid ligament
items.e: The Cedell fracture is an avulsion by the posterior tibiotalar ligament of the deltoid; the lateral tubercle (Shepherd) fracture is avulsed by the posterior talofibular ligament.

items.q: During zone II flexor tendon repair of both FDS and FDP, the repaired tendons are bulky and catch under the A2 pulley. Which is the recommended step?
o: Repair FDP and excise one slip of FDS
Leave FDP unrepaired and repair only FDS
Tenodese the FDP stump to the middle phalanx
items.e: Excising one FDS slip (and, if needed, venting part of A2 or the A4 pulley) reduces bulk and improves glide of the FDP repair while preserving pulley function (Tang).

items.q: Which pair of annular pulleys is most important in preventing bowstringing of the digital flexor tendons?
items.e: A2 (over the proximal phalanx) and A4 (over the middle phalanx) are the largest, bone-attached pulleys and are critical to prevent bowstringing; A1, A3 and A5 lie over joints.

items.q: A 40-year-old woman treated in a cast for an undisplaced distal radius fracture suddenly cannot extend her thumb IP joint at 6 weeks. Which tendon has most likely ruptured?
items.e: EPL ruptures by attrition or ischaemia in the third compartment around Lister's tubercle, typically after undisplaced fractures; EIP transfer is the usual reconstruction.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman has nocturnal numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers relieved by shaking the hand; sensation over the thenar eminence is normal. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
items.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome is confirmed by NCS showing prolonged median distal sensory/motor latency across the wrist; thenar sensation is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the carpal tunnel.

items.q: A young man treated for a closed distal radius fracture develops increasing tingling of the radial three digits and weak thumb opposition. Which nerve is most likely compressed?
items.e: Acute or delayed carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest nerve complication of distal radius fractures; the AIN is purely motor and does not affect sensation or thenar opposition.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a recognised site of median nerve compression around the elbow and proximal forearm (pronator syndrome)?
o: Between the heads of pronator teres
items.e: Pronator syndrome compression sites are the ligament of Struthers, lacertus fibrosus, the two heads of pronator teres and the FDS arch; pronator quadratus is in the distal forearm and does not compress the median nerve.

items.q: A 24-year-old motorcyclist has weak shoulder abduction and elbow flexion with normal wrist and finger extension. Which roots are most likely injured?
items.e: Upper plexus (Erb) injury involves C5–C6, producing the waiter's-tip posture; involvement of C7 would add weakness of wrist and finger extension.

items.q: A volleyball player has isolated weakness of shoulder external rotation; MRI shows a paralabral cyst at the spinoglenoid notch. EMG would show denervation of which muscle(s)?
items.e: At the spinoglenoid notch the suprascapular nerve has already supplied supraspinatus, so only infraspinatus is affected; compression at the suprascapular notch affects both muscles.

items.q: Which nerve is most commonly injured in an anterior shoulder dislocation?
items.e: The axillary nerve passes below the glenohumeral joint through the quadrangular space and is stretched by the anteroinferiorly displaced humeral head; it is the commonest nerve injury, especially in older patients.

items.q: A 27‑year‑old college athlete presents with wrist pain after a forearm twist injury. On examination the anatomical snuffbox is tender and axial thumb compression reproduces pain. Plain radiographs are normal. Which imaging modality is most appropriate to rule out an occult scaphoid fracture?
items.e: MRI is the gold‑standard for occult scaphoid fractures, giving near 100 % sensitivity and specificity, especially within the first few days of injury.

items.q: A lateral wrist radiograph shows a scapholunate angle of 75° with the lunate tilted dorsally. Which instability pattern is this?
