items.e: A scapholunate angle >60° with dorsal lunate tilt (radiolunate >15°) indicates DISI, typically from scapholunate ligament disruption; VISI shows a volar-flexed lunate and an SL angle <30°.

items.q: The SWIFFT trial (Lancet 2020) studied adults with scaphoid waist fractures displaced ≤2 mm. What did it conclude?
o: Early screw fixation gave better 52-week wrist function
Cast immobilisation with urgent fixation of confirmed non-unions gave equivalent outcomes
Surgery eliminated non-union and should be routine
Below-elbow casting had a higher non-union rate than thumb spica
items.e: SWIFFT found no clinically important difference in PRWE at 52 weeks between early fixation and casting (with fixation of non-unions), and surgery had more complications, so casting is recommended for these fractures.

items.q: A 24-year-old who cleans a home aquarium develops chronic nodular lesions and tenosynovitis of the hand that do not respond to standard antibiotics. Which organism and regimen are most appropriate?
o: Mycobacterium marinum – clarithromycin with ethambutol (± rifampicin)
items.e: Fish-tank exposure with chronic granulomatous tenosynovitis suggests M. marinum (culture at 30–32°C); deep infection needs months of combination therapy with clarithromycin and ethambutol, often rifampicin, plus synovectomy.

items.q: In the Swanson (IFSSH) classification of congenital hand anomalies, simple syndactyly belongs to which group?
items.e: Swanson group II, failure of differentiation, includes syndactyly, camptodactyly, clinodactyly and radioulnar synostosis; the OMT classification is now preferred by the IFSSH.

items.q: A newborn has a V-shaped cleft in the centre of the hand with absence of the middle finger ray; the feet are similarly affected and the father has the same deformity. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Typical cleft hand is V-shaped, often bilateral with foot involvement and autosomal dominant; symbrachydactyly (atypical cleft) is U-shaped, unilateral, with small nubbins and no foot involvement.

items.q: A Caucasian infant has bilateral postaxial polydactyly of the hands, short limbs, dysplastic nails and an atrial septal defect. Which syndrome is most likely?
items.e: Ellis–van Creveld (chondroectodermal dysplasia, EVC/EVC2) causes postaxial polydactyly, short-limb dwarfism, ectodermal dysplasia and cardiac defects; postaxial polydactyly in Caucasians warrants a search for such syndromes.

items.q: In a diabetic patient with a foot ulcer, why is the toe-brachial index more reliable than the ankle-brachial index for assessing perfusion?
o: Digital arteries are relatively spared from medial arterial calcification
The TBI measures tissue oxygen tension
The TBI is unaffected by proximal arterial stenosis
items.e: Medial calcinosis makes tibial arteries incompressible and falsely raises the ABI, whereas digital arteries are usually spared; a TBI below 0.7 is abnormal.

items.q: Increased talar tilt on a varus stress radiograph of the ankle mainly indicates insufficiency of which ligament, in addition to the ATFL?
items.e: The ATFL resists anterior translation in plantarflexion, while the CFL resists inversion (talar tilt) in neutral; tilt >10° or >5° more than the other side suggests combined ATFL–CFL insufficiency.

items.q: What is the most common cause of end-stage ankle arthritis?
items.e: About 70–80% of end-stage ankle arthritis is post-traumatic (after fractures or recurrent instability), unlike the hip and knee where primary OA predominates.

items.q: Which radiographic view best shows the talar neck for assessing fracture displacement?
o: Canale view (maximum equinus, 15° pronation, beam 15° cephalad)
items.e: The Canale view profiles the talar neck and shows varus malalignment and comminution; the Broden view shows the posterior facet of the subtalar joint and the Harris view the calcaneal tuberosity.

items.q: A rugby player's finger is forcibly extended while gripping an opponent's jersey; he cannot flex the DIP joint. Which tendon is most commonly avulsed in this injury?
items.e: Jersey finger (FDP avulsion from forced extension of the actively flexed digit) involves the ring finger in about 75% of cases, as it is the most prominent fingertip in grip.

items.q: In a two-stage (Hunter) flexor tendon reconstruction, what is implanted at the first stage?
items.e: Stage 1 places a silicone rod (with pulley reconstruction) to form a pseudosheath; at stage 2, about 3 months later, the rod is replaced with a tendon graft such as palmaris longus or plantaris.

items.q: Which blood vessel provides retrograde arterial supply to approximately 70% to 80% of the scaphoid (including its proximal pole) by entering the non-articular dorsal ridge at the waist?
o: Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
Dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery
Deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
items.e: According to Gelberman, the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters the dorsal ridge at the waist to supply about 70-80% of the scaphoid by retrograde flow, putting the proximal pole at high risk of AVN. The superficial palmar branch supplies only the distal 20-30%.

items.q: A 28-year-old male has an ununited proximal pole scaphoid fracture without secondary arthritic changes. Intraoperatively, after curettage of the non-union interface, no punctate bleeding is observed from the proximal fragment, confirming avascular necrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Pedicled vascularised bone graft based on the 1,2-intercompartmental supraretinacular artery (1,2-ICSRA)
Non-vascularised cancellous bone graft with percutaneous headless screw fixation
items.e: The absence of punctate bleeding at surgery is the most reliable intraoperative indicator of proximal pole avascular necrosis. For an ununited scaphoid with proximal pole AVN and no arthritis, a vascularised bone graft such as the pedicled 1,2-ICSRA graft (Zaidemberg) is indicated.

items.q: A 28-year-old painter accidentally injects industrial oil-based paint under high pressure (8,000 kPa) into the tip of his non-dominant index finger. On initial examination 2 hours post-injury, there is only a tiny pinhole lesion at the pulp with minimal discomfort. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Local wound care, oral broad-spectrum antibiotics, and outpatient review in 48 hours
High-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy and ice pack application
Immediate operative decompression and wide surgical debridement within 6 hours
Closed catheter irrigation of the pulp space under local anaesthesia
items.e: High-pressure injection injuries, particularly with oil-based paints, are surgical emergencies that require wide surgical decompression and debridement within 6 hours to prevent severe chemical necrosis and secondary amputation.

items.q: A 40-year-old bartender presents with chronic swelling, erythema, and loss of the cuticle affecting multiple fingernails for 3 months due to Candida albicans infection. Conservative management with topical antifungals has failed. What is the surgical procedure of choice for refractory chronic paronychia?
o: High lateral mid-axial incision on the non-contact side of the digit
Eponychial marsupialisation (crescent excision of the dorsal eponychial fold)
Complete nail bed ablation using chemical cautery
Longitudinal incision across the pulp space extending proximal to the DIP crease
items.e: Eponychial marsupialisation, which involves a crescent-shaped excision of the dorsal eponychial fold (with or without nail plate removal), is the definitive surgical procedure for chronic paronychia refractory to medical management.

items.q: A 26-year-old dental hygienist presents with intense, throbbing right index fingertip pain. Physical examination shows a cluster of clear vesicles on an erythematous, non-tense pulp. A Tzanck smear reveals multinucleated giant cells. What is the most appropriate management?
o: High-pressure closed irrigation of the digital pulp
Urgent incision and drainage via a mid-axial incision
Wide surgical debridement and bony curettage of the distal phalanx
Non-operative management with a protective dressing and oral acyclovir
items.e: Herpetic whitlow is a viral infection that must be managed non-operatively with protective dressings and oral acyclovir; surgical incision is contraindicated because it increases the risk of secondary bacterial infection and systemic viraemia.

items.q: A 55-year-old diabetic male presents with necrotising fasciitis of the left upper limb. In addition to broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage and urgent radical surgical debridement, which intravenous antibiotic is included specifically to suppress bacterial exotoxin production?
items.e: Clindamycin is added to broad-spectrum intravenous empiric coverage in necrotising fasciitis to inhibit protein synthesis and suppress exotoxin production by streptococcal and staphylococcal pathogens.

items.q: A 48-year-old patient presents with a painless, slowly enlarging dumbbell-shaped swelling in the palm and distal forearm that demonstrates cross-fluctuation across the flexor retinaculum. Surgical exploration reveals numerous small, smooth, white 'rice bodies' within the distended synovial bursae. What is the diagnosis?
o: Acute pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis due to Staphylococcus aureus
items.e: Tuberculous tenosynovitis of the hand (compound palmar ganglion) classicially presents as an hourglass or dumbbell swelling with cross-fluctuation across the flexor retinaculum, containing characteristic fibrin 'rice bodies' within the flexor sheaths.

items.q: A newborn infant is evaluated for a rare congenital difference characterized by duplication of the ulnar structures, including eight fingers and absence of a thumb (mirror hand / ulnar dimelia). Alteration in which signalling centre and molecule is responsible for this anterior-posterior axis defect?
o: Apical ectodermal ridge (AER) / Fibroblast growth factor-8 (FGF-8)
Zone of polarising activity (ZPA) / Sonic hedgehog (SHH)
items.e: Anterior-posterior (radial-ulnar) limb patterning is governed by the Zone of Polarising Activity (ZPA) via Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signalling. Duplication of the ZPA or ectopic SHH expression leads to ulnar dimelia (mirror hand).

items.q: A 10-month-old infant with Type IV radial longitudinal deficiency (complete absence of the radius) is being evaluated for wrist centralisation. Which clinical finding serves as an absolute contraindication to centralisation?
items.e: A stiff elbow in extension is a strict contraindication to wrist centralisation. Patients with fixed elbow extension rely on the radial deviation at the wrist to bring the hand to the mouth for feeding.

items.q: During a Buck-Gramcko pollicisation of the index finger for Type IIIB thumb hypoplasia, which intrinsic muscle of the index finger is transposed to function as the new abductor pollicis brevis (APB)?
items.e: In Buck-Gramcko pollicisation, the first dorsal interosseous muscle of the index finger is reattached to function as the abductor pollicis brevis (APB), while the first palmar interosseous is reattached to serve as the adductor pollicis.

items.q: Which of the following features accurately distinguishes typical central cleft hand from symbrachydactyly?
o: Cleft hand is typically sporadic and strictly unilateral
Cleft hand has a V-shaped central cleft, autosomal dominant inheritance, and frequent bilateral foot involvement
Cleft hand features short U-shaped digit nubbins with rudimentary nails
Cleft hand is strongly associated with Poland syndrome
items.e: Typical central cleft hand presents as a V-shaped central deficiency with autosomal dominant inheritance, high penetrance, bilateral hand involvement, and frequent foot involvement (split hand-foot malformation). Symbrachydactyly is sporadic, unilateral, U-shaped, and associated with Poland syndrome.

items.q: A 4-year-old child presents with radial angular deformity of the little finger at the DIP joint. Radiographs confirm a triangular middle phalanx with a longitudinal epiphyseal bracket (delta phalanx). Which procedure is indicated to allow progressive alignment and longitudinal growth?
o: Opening-wedge osteotomy of the distal phalanx
Vickers physiolysis (excision of the longitudinal epiphyseal bracket with fat interposition)
items.e: In young children (under 6 years) with clinodactyly due to a delta phalanx, Vickers physiolysis—resecting the continuous longitudinal bracket of the C-shaped physis and interposing fat—allows normal growth from the remaining epiphyses to correct the deformity.

items.q: A 14-year-old girl evaluated for wrist pain and deformity shows volar and ulnar tilt of the distal radial articular surface and a dorsally prominent ulnar head (Madelung deformity). What is the primary soft-tissue tethering structure implicated in this condition?
items.e: Madelung deformity is driven by an abnormal volar-ulnar tether of the distal radial physis caused by Vickers ligament (an anomalous thick radiolunate ligament), which restricts normal physeal growth at the volar-ulnar corner.

items.q: A 46-year-old male presents with bilateral palmar Dupuytren disease, plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease), and dorsal PIP joint cutaneous nodules (Garrod knuckle pads). Which feature is characteristic of Hueston Dupuytren diathesis?
o: Late onset of disease after 70 years of age
Presence of ectopic lesions such as Garrod knuckle pads and Ledderhose disease
Exclusive involvement of the radial digits in female patients
items.e: Dupuytren diathesis (Hueston) represents aggressive disease with a high recurrence rate and is characterized by early onset (< 50 years), positive family history, bilateral disease, male sex, Northern European ethnicity, radial-sided disease, and ectopic fibromatosis (Garrod knuckle pads, Ledderhose disease, Peyronie disease).

items.q: A 64-year-old man presents with a flexion deformity of the ring finger. Clinical examination reveals a 35-degree flexion contracture at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint and a positive Hueston tabletop test. Which of the following is an established indication for intervention in Dupuytren disease?
o: Presence of an isolated non-tender palmar nodule without contracture
MCP joint flexion contracture of 30 degrees or more
PIP joint flexion contracture of less than 5 degrees
items.e: Indications for intervention in Dupuytren disease include an MCP joint contracture of 30 degrees or more, any PIP joint contracture (of about 15–20 degrees or more), and a positive Hueston tabletop test. Palmar nodules without joint contracture are not an indication for procedure.

items.q: According to established management principles for surgical reconstruction in the rheumatoid hand and wrist, which sequence of operative intervention is recommended?
o: Finger deformities should be corrected prior to stabilizing the wrist joint
Wrist stabilization should be performed before finger reconstruction
Tendon transfers should precede joint stabilization
Upper limb joint procedures should precede lower limb joint procedures
items.e: General surgical priorities in rheumatoid arthritis require treating the lower limb before the upper limb, proximal joints before distal joints, and stabilizing the wrist before performing finger reconstruction, because a stable wrist provides the necessary foundation for finger function.

items.q: A 58-year-old patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with a thumb deformity characterized by MCP joint flexion and IP joint hyperextension. What is the Nalebuff classification for this deformity, which represents the most common thumb deformity in rheumatoid arthritis?
items.e: Nalebuff Type I thumb deformity (boutonniere thumb) is the most common thumb deformity in rheumatoid arthritis (accounting for 50–70% of cases). MCP joint synovitis stretches the EPB insertion, resulting in MCP joint flexion and secondary IP joint hyperextension.

items.q: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with severe ulnar drift and swan-neck deformities of her fingers. On physical examination, all deformities are completely and easily reducible manually. Radiographs show normal joint spaces without articular erosions. Which statement regarding hand involvement in this patient (Jaccoud arthropathy) is correct?
o: Deformities are caused by severe marginal cartilage destruction and erosions
Soft-tissue rebalancing procedures have high success rates with minimal recurrence
Deformities are driven by severe capsuloligamentous laxity without joint destruction
Immediate silastic MCP joint replacement is the treatment of choice
items.e: Jaccoud arthropathy in SLE is caused by severe capsuloligamentous laxity leading to reducible deformities (ulnar drift, swan-neck) without intrinsic joint destruction or erosion. Soft-tissue reconstruction procedures carry a high failure/recurrence rate due to persistent laxity, making arthrodesis preferred when surgery is needed.

items.q: During hallux valgus development, the first metatarsal head drifts medially while the sesamoids appear laterally displaced on radiographs. Which anatomical structures anchor the sesamoids in their anatomical position relative to the second metatarsal?
o: Abductor hallucis and long extensor tendons
Adductor hallucis and transverse metatarsal ligament
Flexor hallucis brevis medial head and plantaris tendon
Medial sesamoid ligament and abductor hallucis
items.e: The sesamoids remain anchored in their anatomical position relative to the second metatarsal by the adductor hallucis tendon and the transverse metatarsal ligament, while the first metatarsal head drifts medially off the sesamoids.

items.q: A 16-year-old female presents with symptomatic juvenile hallux valgus. Radiographs reveal parallel articular surfaces of the first MTP joint (congruent deformity) with an increased distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA). Which management principle is correct?
o: Soft-tissue release alone is sufficient to restore alignment
Perform Keller resection arthroplasty to reduce joint congruency
Correction must not be done by soft-tissue release alone; use a DMAA-correcting osteotomy such as a biplanar chevron
Perform an immediate first MTP joint arthrodesis regardless of skeletal maturity
items.e: In a congruent joint with an increased DMAA, soft-tissue release alone would create an incongruent joint. A DMAA-correcting osteotomy (such as a biplanar chevron) or extra-articular osteotomy must be used.

items.q: A 54-year-old runner has advanced hallux rigidus (Coughlin and Shurnas Grade 4) with a positive grind test and severe pain in mid-range motion. What is the gold-standard surgical procedure and its optimal sagittal position relative to the floor?
o: First MTPJ arthrodesis; 10 to 15 degrees dorsiflexion relative to the floor
items.e: First MTPJ arthrodesis is the gold standard for Coughlin and Shurnas grade 3 and 4 hallux rigidus. The optimal position is about 10–15 degrees of valgus, 10–15 degrees of dorsiflexion relative to the floor (20–25 degrees relative to the first metatarsal shaft), and neutral rotation.

items.q: During a dorsal surgical approach for neurectomy of a primary Morton neuroma in the third web space, which ligament must be divided and how far proximal to this ligament should the nerve be resected?
o: Deep transverse metatarsal ligament; resect the nerve about 3 cm proximal to the ligament
Interosseous fascia; resect the nerve flush with the metatarsal head
Plantar aponeurosis; resect the nerve 5 cm proximal to the metatarsal neck
Superficial transverse metatarsal ligament; resect the nerve 0.5 cm distal to the ligament
items.e: During dorsal neurectomy for Morton neuroma, the deep transverse metatarsal ligament is divided and the nerve is resected approximately 3 cm proximal to the ligament to prevent symptomatic stump neuroma formation in the weight-bearing area.

items.q: A patient presents with bilateral lesser toe deformities affecting multiple digits. Clinical examination reveals hyperextension at the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints combined with flexion at both the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. Which deformity is present and what is its primary underlying mechanism?
o: Hammer toe; FDL tight contraction with neutral MTP joint alignment
Curly toe; congenital extensor tendon tightness
items.e: Claw toe deformity consists of MTP joint hyperextension combined with PIP and DIP joint flexion. It usually involves multiple toes bilaterally in patients with neuromuscular conditions or cavus feet due to intrinsic muscle weakness.

items.q: A 48-year-old female evaluated for forefoot metatarsalgia has limited ankle dorsiflexion when the knee is in full extension, but normal dorsiflexion is restored when the knee is flexed to 90 degrees. What is this clinical finding and the corresponding surgical intervention?
o: Positive Lachman test; flexor-to-extensor tendon transfer
Positive Silfverskiöld test; gastrocnemius recession (Strayer procedure)
Positive Mulder click; proximal 1st metatarsal osteotomy
Positive grind test; PIP joint resection arthroplasty (DuVries)
items.e: A positive Silfverskiöld test indicates isolated gastrocnemius tightness (ankle dorsiflexion is limited with the knee extended but improves with knee flexion). The treatment for refractory cases is gastrocnemius recession (Strayer procedure).

items.q: A 52-year-old obese woman presents with medial ankle pain and a progressive flatfoot deformity. Examination reveals a flexible hindfoot valgus, a positive 'too many toes' sign with forefoot abduction showing >40% talonavicular uncoverage, and inability to perform a single-limb heel rise. Radiographs confirm severe forefoot abduction without fixed joint arthrosis. According to the Johnson and Strom classification (modified), which stage is this patient, and what is the appropriate joint-sparing operative strategy?
o: Stage I; Tenosynovectomy and immobilisation in a short leg cast
Stage IIB; FDL transfer to navicular + medializing calcaneal osteotomy + Evans lateral column lengthening
Stage III; Triple arthrodesis through medial and lateral incisions
Stage IVA; Deltoid ligament reconstruction + tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis
items.e: The patient has Stage IIB adult acquired flatfoot deformity (dysfunctional TP tendon, flexible flatfoot with forefoot abduction >30-40% talonavicular uncoverage). Joint-sparing reconstruction for Stage IIB combines FDL transfer to the navicular, medializing displacement calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO), and Evans lateral column lengthening.

items.q: A 24-year-old man with progressive bilateral high-arched feet and hindfoot varus undergoes clinical evaluation. A Coleman block test is performed: with a block placed under the lateral heel and lateral forefoot, the first metatarsal head drops off the medial edge, resulting in complete manual correction of the hindfoot varus to neutral. What is the correct interpretation and primary surgical plan for the forefoot?
o: Fixed hindfoot-driven deformity; requires lateral closing-wedge calcaneal (Dwyer) osteotomy
Forefoot-driven flexible hindfoot deformity; requires dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal base and plantar fascia release
Ankle instability; requires isolated Broström lateral ligament reconstruction
Rigid midfoot cavus; requires Cole dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy alone
items.e: Correction of hindfoot varus during the Coleman block test confirms a flexible, forefoot-driven cavus deformity (driven by a plantarflexed first ray). Management focuses on forefoot procedures: dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal base and plantar fascia release.

items.q: A 45-year-old long-distance runner presents with chronic medial heel pain refractory to non-operative treatment for plantar fasciitis. MRI of the foot reveals fatty infiltration and atrophy localized specifically to the abductor digiti minimi muscle. Which nerve is entrapped?
o: Baxter nerve (first branch of lateral plantar nerve / inferior calcaneal nerve)
items.e: Baxter nerve (first branch of the lateral plantar nerve or inferior calcaneal nerve) entrapment causes chronic medial heel pain mimicking plantar fasciitis and characteristically leads to atrophy of the abductor digiti minimi muscle on MRI.

items.q: Which radiographic feature on a weight-bearing lateral foot radiograph is characteristic of pes cavus rather than flatfoot deformity?
o: Lateral talo-first metatarsal (Meary) angle with plantar convexity >4 degrees
Calcaneal pitch angle reduced below 20 degrees
Lateral talo-first metatarsal (Meary) angle convex dorsally (negative angle less than -4 degrees)
AP talonavicular uncoverage percentage greater than 40%
items.e: In pes cavus, the lateral talo-first metatarsal (Meary) angle is convex dorsally (negative angle < -4 degrees) and calcaneal pitch is increased (>30 degrees). Plantar convexity of Meary angle >4 degrees and reduced calcaneal pitch indicate flatfoot.

items.q: A patient underwent an Evans lateral column lengthening procedure for stage II adult acquired flatfoot deformity. Postoperatively, the patient reports severe new-onset pain over the lateral midfoot during weight bearing. Which complication is most specifically associated with lateral column lengthening?
o: Tarsal tunnel syndrome from medial nerve traction
Lateral column overload and calcaneocuboid joint arthritis
Avascular necrosis of the medial cuneiform
items.e: Lateral column lengthening (Evans osteotomy) increases force across the lateral midfoot, making lateral column overload (lateral foot pain) and calcaneocuboid (CC) joint arthritis the most common specific complications.

items.q: A 28-year-old patient with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease presents with a painful, flexible cock-up claw deformity of the hallux causing dorsal interphalangeal joint skin callosities. Which operative procedure is specifically designed to correct this hallux deformity?
o: Jones transfer (extensor hallucis longus transfer to first metatarsal neck + hallux IP joint fusion)
Hibbs transfer (extensor digitorum longus transfer to lateral cuneiform)
Steindler release of the plantar fascia
Peroneus longus to peroneus brevis tendon transfer
items.e: The Jones transfer involves transferring the extensor hallucis longus (EHL) tendon to the neck of the first metatarsal combined with arthrodesis of the hallux interphalangeal (IP) joint, specifically indicated for a clawed hallux in pes cavus.

items.q: A 38-year-old recreational athlete presents with calf pain after a sudden push-off during a game. On physical examination with the patient prone and knees flexed to 90 degrees, the injured foot assumes a neutral to dorsiflexed position compared to the normal resting plantarflexed foot on the contralateral side. Which clinical test is described?
items.e: The Matles test assesses the loss of resting plantarflexion tension in an acute Achilles tendon rupture; with the patient prone and knees flexed to 90 degrees, an injured foot hangs in neutral or dorsiflexion instead of the normal mild equinus posture. The Simmonds-Thompson test is the calf squeeze test, while the Royal London Hospital test is used for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.

items.q: A 48-year-old male presents with a neglected Achilles tendon rupture of 8 weeks duration. MRI reveals a 4 cm gap between the retracted tendon ends after debridement of scar tissue. According to Myerson's classification and surgical algorithm for chronic Achilles ruptures, what is the recommended procedure for a gap of this size (2 to 5 cm)?
o: V-Y lengthening of the gastrocnemius aponeurosis with or without FHL transfer
Flexor hallucis longus (FHL) transfer alone with an anchor into the calcaneus
items.e: According to Myerson's management protocol for chronic Achilles ruptures, gaps under 1–2 cm are treated with end-to-end repair, gaps of 2–5 cm are treated with V-Y lengthening of the gastrocnemius aponeurosis (with or without FHL transfer), and gaps greater than 5 cm are managed with FHL transfer (plus turndown flap or graft).

items.q: During a minimally invasive percutaneous repair of an acute Achilles tendon rupture, lateral suture pass placement carries a high risk of iatrogenic nerve injury. At what approximate distance proximal to its calcaneal insertion does the sural nerve cross from medial to lateral relative to the Achilles tendon?
items.e: The sural nerve crosses from medial to lateral and comes to lie immediately lateral to the Achilles tendon at approximately 10 cm proximal to its insertion on the calcaneus. This makes it particularly vulnerable during lateral surgical incisions and percutaneous suture passes in Achilles repairs.

items.q: A 34-year-old runner with a cavovarus foot deformity presents with chronic lateral ankle pain and focal tenderness posterior to the fibula. MRI demonstrates a longitudinal split tear of the peroneus brevis tendon involving approximately 30% of its cross-sectional area. Which surgical management is indicated for this tendon defect?
o: Complete excision of the peroneus brevis and tenodesis to the peroneus longus
Debridement and tubularisation of the peroneus brevis tendon
Excision of the os peroneum and SPR release
items.e: For longitudinal split tears of the peroneus brevis tendon involving less than 50% of the cross-sectional area, debridement of the tear edges and tubularisation of the tendon is recommended. If more than 50% of the tendon cross-section is compromised, tenodesis to the peroneus longus is indicated.

items.q: During posterior ankle arthroscopy for excision of a symptomatic os trigonum in a ballet dancer, which structure serves as the key anatomical landmark that the surgeon must stay lateral to in order to avoid damaging the tibial neurovascular bundle?
items.e: During posterior ankle arthroscopy (performed using prone posterolateral and posteromedial portals), the flexor hallucis longus (FHL) tendon is the crucial anatomical landmark. Remaining lateral to the FHL protects the tibial neurovascular bundle, which lies medial to the FHL tunnel.

items.q: A patient undergoing anterior ankle arthroscopy for anterior ankle impingement develops postoperative numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most commonly at risk when establishing the anterolateral portal?
o: Superficial peroneal nerve (intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch)
items.e: The intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial peroneal nerve is at highest risk during anterolateral portal placement in anterior ankle arthroscopy, making superficial peroneal nerve injury the most common complication of ankle arthroscopy. The anterocentral portal is avoided because it risks the dorsalis pedis artery and deep peroneal nerve.

items.q: A 60-year-old neuropathic diabetic patient presents with an uninfected, superficial plantar ulcer beneath the head of the second metatarsal. Peripheral pulses are intact. Which offloading modality is considered the gold standard for promoting wound healing in this patient?
o: Custom extra-depth therapeutic footwear with insoles
Felted foam dressings with surgical shoe
items.e: Total contact casting (TCC) is the gold standard offloading modality for non-infected neuropathic plantar foot ulcers, forcing compliance and achieving healing rates of 80–90% within 6–8 weeks. TCC is contraindicated in the presence of active infection or severe peripheral arterial disease.

items.q: A 52-year-old diabetic patient presents with a hot, red, swollen midfoot following minor trauma. Plain weight-bearing radiographs of the foot are entirely normal, but MRI demonstrates extensive subchondral bone marrow edema and microfractures. According to the Eichenholtz (and modified Shibata) classification of Charcot neuroarthropathy, this clinical scenario represents:
items.e: Stage 0 (Shibata stage) represents the active prodromal or 'at-risk' inflammatory phase where clinical signs of warmth and edema are present with normal plain radiographs, but MRI reveals diagnostic bone marrow edema and microfractures. Radiographic fragmentation appears later in Stage I.

items.q: According to the Brodsky anatomical classification of Charcot neuroarthropathy, which region is most commonly involved, accounting for approximately 60% to 70% of cases?
o: Type 2: Hindfoot (subtalar, talonavicular, and calcaneocuboid joints)
items.e: Brodsky Type 1 involves the tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) and naviculocuneiform midfoot joints and is the most common anatomical site (60–70%), frequently leading to a classic rocker-bottom deformity with midfoot plantar ulceration.

items.q: Percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening (Hoke technique) is performed as an adjunctive procedure in a diabetic patient to lower peak forefoot plantar pressures and treat a chronic plantar ulcer. What is the most common secondary complication associated with overlengthening the heel cord in this clinical scenario?
o: Transfer ulceration to the calcaneus / heel
Rigid dorsiflexion contracture of the first MTP joint
items.e: Overlengthening of the Achilles tendon reduces forefoot pressure but shifts load to the posterior heel, potentially causing a calcaneus gait deformity and transfer ulceration over the calcanean tuberosity.

items.q: Which of the following is a key technical principle of 'superconstruct' fixation as described by Sammarco for surgical reconstruction of unstable Charcot foot deformities?
o: Arthrodesis limited strictly to hypermobile joints, deliberately avoiding adjacent normal joints
Extending fixation and fusion beyond the zone of injury to include uninvolved healthy joints
Application of internal hardware exclusively along the dorsal anatomical tension side
Avoiding bone resection to preserve maximal skeletal length regardless of soft tissue tension
items.e: Sammarco's 'superconstruct' principles for Charcot reconstruction include: 1) extending fusion beyond the zone of injury into intact adjacent joints; 2) performing adequate bone resection to decompress soft tissues; 3) placing the strongest hardware tolerated; and 4) placing hardware in the optimal mechanical position (such as plantar plating).

items.q: A 22-year-old athlete presents to the emergency department after an inversion injury to his ankle during a basketball match. On examination, he has swelling and ecchymosis over the anterolateral ankle. There is no bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus (distal 6 cm), no tenderness over the navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal, and he is able to bear weight for 4 steps in the emergency department. According to the Ottawa Ankle Rules, which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Obtain weight-bearing radiographs of the ankle immediately
Initiate non-operative functional treatment without ankle radiographs
Perform acute surgical repair of the anterior talofibular ligament
Apply a strict non-weight-bearing below-knee cast for 6 weeks
items.e: According to the Ottawa Ankle Rules, radiographs are required only if there is pain in the malleolar zone along with bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus (distal 6 cm) or an inability to bear weight for 4 steps immediately and in the emergency department. Since none of these criteria are present, radiographs are not indicated, and functional treatment (protection, early mobilisation, and strengthening) should be initiated.

items.q: During surgical exposure of the lateral ankle, a resident is asked to identify the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL). Which anatomical description of the CFL is correct?
o: It is an intracapsular ligament that is taut in plantarflexion
It originates 1 cm proximal to the tip of the fibula and attaches to the talar neck
It is an extracapsular ligament deep to the peroneal tendons that is taut in dorsiflexion
It is the weakest component of the lateral complex and is injured first in inversion sprains
items.e: The calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) is extracapsular, located deep to the peroneal tendons (forming the floor of the peroneal sheath), taut in dorsiflexion, and resists inversion in neutral/dorsiflexion. In contrast, the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is intracapsular, taut in plantarflexion, and is the weakest and most commonly/first injured lateral ligament.

items.q: A 28-year-old runner with chronic mechanical lateral ankle instability has persistent symptomatic laxity despite completing 6 months of supervised peroneal strengthening and proprioceptive training. MRI reveals good remaining tissue quality and no severe deformity. What is the surgical procedure of choice?
o: Anatomic reconstruction using a free gracilis tendon graft
items.e: The modified Broström-Gould procedure (anatomic repair via imbrication/shortening of the ATFL and CFL reinforced with the inferior extensor retinaculum) is the gold standard for chronic lateral ankle instability, achieving 85–95% good results. Non-anatomic tenodeses (Watson-Jones, Chrisman-Snook) are historical procedures associated with subtalar stiffness, while free tendon autografts are reserved for failed Broström repairs, hyperlaxity, or poor tissue quality.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman undergoes an open modified Broström-Gould repair for chronic lateral ankle instability. Postoperatively, she reports numbness and dysesthesia over the dorsum of her foot. Which nerve is most susceptible to injury during this procedure?
items.e: Superficial peroneal nerve injury is the most common nerve complication associated with lateral ankle ligament repair and reconstruction procedures (modified Broström-Gould). Sural nerve injury can also occur, but superficial peroneal nerve injury occurs most frequently.

items.q: A 48-year-old manual laborer presents with painful varus ankle osteoarthritis. Weight-bearing radiographs show Takakura Stage 2 medial joint space narrowing with at least 50% of the joint space preserved. There is no panarthritis or severe talar tilt. Which joint-preserving surgical procedure is indicated?
items.e: Supramalleolar osteotomy (SMOT), such as a medial opening-wedge tibial osteotomy for varus OA, is indicated in younger, active patients with asymmetric ankle osteoarthritis who have at least 50% of the joint surface preserved (Takakura 2–3A). It restores alignment and can delay fusion or replacement by about 10 years.

items.q: During an ankle arthrodesis for end-stage post-traumatic arthritis, what is the optimal position for surgical fusion of the ankle joint?
o: 10° equinus, 5° hindfoot varus, 15° internal rotation, anterior talar translation
5° dorsiflexion, 10° hindfoot varus, 0° rotation, neutral talar translation
10° equinus, 5° hindfoot valgus, 5° external rotation, anterior talar translation
Neutral dorsiflexion (90°), 5° hindfoot valgus, 5–10° external rotation, slight posterior talar translation
items.e: The optimal position for ankle arthrodesis is neutral dorsiflexion (90°), 5° hindfoot valgus, external rotation of 5–10° (equal to the contralateral side), and slight posterior translation of the talus. Equinus alignment causes genu recurvatum and knee pain, while hindfoot varus leads to lateral foot overload.

items.q: A 62-year-old patient with severe ankle arthritis is evaluated for total ankle replacement (TAR). Which of the following clinical conditions is an absolute contraindication to performing TAR?
o: Active or recent deep ankle joint infection
items.e: Active or recent deep joint infection is an absolute contraindication to total ankle replacement (TAR). Other contraindications include Charcot neuroarthropathy, large avascular necrosis of the talus, and severe vascular disease. Bilateral ankle OA, rheumatoid arthritis, and adjacent subtalar joint arthritis/fusion are indications for TAR because motion preservation protects adjacent joints.

items.q: A 24-year-old athlete sustains an ankle injury during a forced external rotation and dorsiflexion stress. The Kleiger test is positive. Anteroposterior radiographs taken 1 cm proximal to the tibial plafond demonstrate a tibiofibular clear space of 8 mm. How should this radiographic finding be interpreted?
o: Normal alignment of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis
Isolated sprain of the calcaneofibular ligament
Isolated injury of the superficial deltoid ligament
items.e: A tibiofibular clear space greater than 6 mm (measured 1 cm proximal to the plafond on AP or mortise views) is the most reliable radiographic indicator of syndesmotic instability/diastasis. The clinical mechanism (external rotation and dorsiflexion) and positive Kleiger test (external rotation stress test, the most sensitive clinical test) confirm a high ankle/syndesmotic sprain.

items.q: A 38-year-old male sustains a Hawkins Type III talar neck fracture with posteromedial extrusion of the talar body. Which of the following vessels is most likely to remain as the solitary source of blood supply to the displaced body fragment, necessitating the preservation of its associated ligament during surgery?
o: Deltoid branch of the artery of the tarsal canal
Posterior recurve branch of the peroneal artery
items.e: The artery of the tarsal canal (from the posterior tibial artery) provides about 50% of the talar body supply. Its deltoid branch supplies the medial body and is often the only remaining supply in displaced neck fractures; preserving the deltoid ligament is crucial to protect this vessel.

items.q: A surgeon is evaluating a talar neck fracture in the emergency department. To accurately assess for varus malreduction and medial comminution, which specific radiographic view, taken with the foot pronated 15 degrees and the tube tilted 75 degrees cephalad, is most appropriate?
items.e: The Canale view is the best radiographic projection for visualizing the talar neck. It is performed with the foot in 15 degrees of pronation and the X-ray beam angled 75 degrees cephalad from the table.

items.q: A 30-year-old athlete presents with a lateral subtalar (peritalar) dislocation. Closed reduction is attempted under sedation but is unsuccessful. Which of the following structures is the most common anatomical block to reduction in this specific injury pattern?
items.e: In lateral subtalar dislocations, the tibialis posterior tendon is the most common structure that becomes interposed and prevents closed reduction. In medial dislocations, the commonest blocks are the talar head buttonholing through the extensor digitorum brevis or the extensor retinaculum.

items.q: On a lateral radiograph of a patient who fell from a height, the surgeon identifies a depressed intra-articular calcaneal fracture. Which of the following sets of measurements would be most characteristic of this injury?
o: Böhler angle of 10 degrees and Gissane angle of 130 degrees
Böhler angle of 35 degrees and Gissane angle of 100 degrees
Böhler angle of 45 degrees and Gissane angle of 80 degrees
Böhler angle of 25 degrees and Gissane angle of 90 degrees
items.e: In calcaneal fractures with posterior facet depression, the Böhler angle (normal 20-40°) decreases or becomes negative, while the critical angle of Gissane (normal 95-105°) typically increases.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with painful scoliosis of the lumbar spine. Physical examination reveals a non-structural curve that is stiff. Radiographs show a small radiolucent lesion in the posterior elements at the apex of the curve on the concave side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Osteoid osteoma characteristically causes painful, non-structural scoliosis when it occurs in the posterior elements of the spine; the lesion is typically located at the apex of the curve on the concave side.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with a slow-growing mass on the posterior aspect of the distal femur. Radiographs reveal a dense, lobulated mass attached to the cortex with a radiolucent 'string sign' (cleavage line) between the tumour and the bone. Which molecular marker is characteristically amplified in this condition?
items.e: The description fits parosteal osteosarcoma (posterior distal femur, women 20-40, string sign). Both parosteal and low-grade central osteosarcoma are characterised by MDM2 and CDK4 amplification.

items.q: According to the established principles of biopsy for suspected bone sarcomas (Mankin rules), which of the following is the correct technique?
o: The biopsy tract should be placed through intermuscular planes to avoid muscle contamination.
Fine needle aspiration (FNA) is the preferred method for histological diagnosis.
The biopsy tract must be oriented in line with the definitive incision to allow en bloc excision.
Drains should be brought out through a separate stab incision at least 5 cm from the biopsy site.
items.e: Biopsy tracts must be placed in line with the definitive incision so they can be removed en bloc. They should go through a single muscle compartment, avoiding intermuscular planes and neurovascular bundles; drains should be brought out in line with the incision.

items.q: A 22-year-old male is found to have multiple dense osteomas on the mandible and skull. Given the high risk of associated systemic conditions, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: MRI of the brain to rule out neurofibromatosis
Bone marrow aspiration for multiple myeloma
items.e: Multiple osteomas of the jaw and skull are associated with Gardner syndrome (FAP), caused by APC gene mutations. Because the colonic polyps have near 100% malignant potential, colonoscopy is indicated.

items.q: Regarding the systemic management of conventional osteosarcoma, which of the following statements is supported by the results of the landmark EURAMOS-1 trial?
o: Intensifying chemotherapy with ifosfamide and etoposide improves outcomes in poor responders.
MAP (Methotrexate, Adriamycin, Cisplatin) remains the standard chemotherapy for all patients.
Pegylated interferon alfa-2b is mandatory for all good responders to prevent relapse.
Post-operative chemotherapy should be changed solely based on the Huvos necrosis grade.
items.e: The EURAMOS-1 trial showed that in poor responders (Huvos <90% necrosis), adding ifosfamide and etoposide to MAP did not improve event-free survival and increased toxicity. MAP remains the standard regimen regardless of response.

items.q: A 12-year-old boy has persistent night pain in the proximal femur, relieved by aspirin. Plain radiographs show cortical thickening but the nidus is not clearly visible. What is the investigation of choice to locate the nidus?
items.e: While bone scans are sensitive (showing the double-density sign), thin-slice CT is the investigation of choice for identifying and precisely locating the radiolucent nidus of an osteoid osteoma.

items.q: A 16-year-old male presents with persistent shoulder pain and a joint effusion. Radiographs show a well-defined lytic lesion in the proximal humeral epiphysis with a thin sclerotic rim. MRI reveals extensive surrounding bone marrow and soft tissue oedema. Which immunohistochemical marker is most specific for this lesion?
items.e: The clinical and radiographic features (epiphyseal location in a skeletally immature patient with 'chicken-wire' calcification and extensive MRI oedema) are classic for chondroblastoma. The H3 K36M (H3F3B) mutation-specific antibody is a highly specific marker for this tumour.

items.q: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with a grade 1 chondrosarcoma of the ilium. What is the most appropriate definitive surgical management for this lesion?
o: Extended intralesional curettage with local adjuvant
items.e: While grade 1 cartilage tumours of the appendicular skeleton are termed 'atypical cartilaginous tumours' (ACT) and can be treated with extended curettage, the term 'grade 1 chondrosarcoma' is retained for axial sites (pelvis, scapula, skull base) where they are more aggressive and require wide en bloc resection.

items.q: Somatic mosaic mutations in IDH1 or IDH2 (isocitrate dehydrogenase) are a characteristic molecular finding in which of the following conditions?
items.e: IDH1 and IDH2 mutations are found in enchondromas, Ollier disease, Maffucci syndrome, and approximately 50% of central conventional chondrosarcomas. HME is associated with EXT1/EXT2 mutations.

items.q: A 40-year-old male presents with a lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the proximal femur. Histology reveals clear cells with distinct borders and scattered osteoclast-like giant cells. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
items.e: Clear cell chondrosarcoma is a low-grade malignant tumour that occurs in the epiphyses of adults (mimicking chondroblastoma). Unlike appendicular ACT, it requires wide en bloc resection because curettage results in high recurrence rates.

items.q: In differentiating a solitary enchondroma from an atypical cartilaginous tumour (ACT) in a long bone, which of the following features most strongly favours a diagnosis of ACT?
o: Endosteal scalloping involving more than two-thirds of the cortical thickness
A lesion size of 3 cm in maximum diameter
items.e: Deep endosteal scalloping (more than two-thirds of the cortical thickness) and a length of scalloping over two-thirds of the lesion are major radiographic features that favour ACT/low-grade chondrosarcoma over a simple enchondroma.

items.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with knee pain and multiple uniform-sized 'rice-grain' calcified bodies within the joint. According to the Milgram classification for synovial chondromatosis, the stage characterized by both active intrasynovial nodules and free loose bodies is:
items.e: Milgram Stage II (transitional phase) is characterized by both active intrasynovial disease (nodules) and the presence of detached loose bodies. Stage I has only intrasynovial disease, and Stage III has loose bodies with quiescent synovium.

items.q: In a patient with a giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB), the neoplastic component that expresses RANK-ligand (RANKL) and carries the characteristic H3F3A (G34W) mutation is the:
o: Endothelial cell of the vascular channels
Foam cell within the reactive stroma
items.e: The mononuclear stromal cells are the neoplastic population in GCTB. They express RANKL, which recruits reactive, RANK-expressing osteoclast-like giant cells that resorb bone. Over 90% of GCTB cases harbor the H3F3A G34W mutation in these stromal cells.

items.q: A 9-year-old boy presents with a sudden onset of pain in the left shoulder after a minor fall. Radiographs show a central, well-defined lytic lesion in the proximal humeral metaphysis that does not extend beyond the physis. A small cortical fragment is seen at the dependent portion of the cyst. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: The 'fallen fragment sign' is pathognomonic for a unicameral bone cyst (UBC). It occurs when a cortical fracture allows a fragment to sink through the fluid-filled cavity. UBCs are typically central and metaphyseal, occurring most commonly in the proximal humerus in children.

items.q: A primary aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is considered a true neoplastic process driven by the rearrangement of which gene?
items.e: Primary ABCs are neoplastic and characterized by USP6 gene rearrangements (commonly CDH11-USP6). Secondary ABCs, which lack this rearrangement, occur in association with other lesions like GCT or chondroblastoma.

items.q: The multicenter randomized controlled trial by Wright et al. (2008) comparing treatments for unicameral bone cysts (UBC) found that:
o: Autologous bone marrow injection was superior to steroid injection
Methylprednisolone acetate injection resulted in higher healing rates than bone marrow injection
All cysts healed completely after a single steroid injection
Flexible intramedullary nailing was the only effective treatment for active cysts
items.e: The Wright et al. (2008) RCT showed that methylprednisolone acetate injections had a significantly higher successful healing rate (42%) compared to autologous bone marrow injections (23%) at 2-year follow-up.

items.q: A 7-year-old presents with back pain and a radiograph showing complete collapse of the T6 vertebral body with preserved adjacent disc spaces ('vertebra plana'). If biopsy reveals cells with grooved 'coffee-bean' nuclei that are CD1a and S100 positive, what is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Vertebra plana (Calvé disease) in a child is a classic presentation of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). The histology (coffee-bean nuclei) and immunohistochemistry (CD1a, S100, CD207) are diagnostic.

items.q: A 24-year-old male presents with wrist pain following a fall onto a dorsiflexed wrist. Radiographs reveal a scaphoid waist fracture with a 1.5 mm step-off and a lateral intrascaphoid angle of 55 degrees. According to current management principles, what is the most appropriate next step?
items.e: Displacement >1 mm and a lateral intrascaphoid angle >45 degrees (humpback deformity) are indicators of an unstable scaphoid fracture. These require reduction and internal fixation to prevent non-union, which occurs in up to 50% of displaced fractures treated with casting.

items.q: Which of the following best describes the primary blood supply to the proximal pole of the scaphoid?
o: Antegrade flow from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
Retrograde flow from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery
Antegrade flow from the volar carpal branch of the radial artery
Retrograde flow from the ulnar artery
items.e: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters the dorsal ridge at the scaphoid waist and provides 70-80% of the blood supply, including the proximal pole, via retrograde flow. This explains the high risk of AVN in proximal pole fractures.

items.q: A patient presents with chronic wrist pain and a suspected scapholunate dissociation. On examination, applying thumb pressure to the scaphoid tubercle while moving the wrist from ulnar to radial deviation produces a painful 'clunk'. This clinical finding is known as:
items.e: The Watson scaphoid shift test is positive when the scaphoid subluxes dorsally over the radial rim and then reduces with a 'clunk' as pressure is released or the wrist is moved, indicating scapholunate ligament insufficiency.

items.q: During the evaluation of a perilunate injury, the 'Space of Poirier' is identified as a critical anatomical weak area. Between which two structures does this space lie?
o: Dorsal intercarpal and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments
items.e: The Space of Poirier is an inherent area of weakness on the volar aspect of the wrist, located between the radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments, over the capitolunate joint. Perilunate dislocations occur through this space.

items.q: A 35-year-old patient with a chronic scaphoid proximal pole non-union is found to have no punctate bleeding from the proximal fragment during surgery. MRI shows evidence of avascular necrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical treatment?
o: Matti-Russe volar inlay cancellous bone graft
items.e: Proximal pole non-union with AVN (confirmed by lack of punctate bleeding) requires a vascularized bone graft. The 1,2-ICSRA (Zaidemberg) graft is the most common pedicled option; non-vascularized grafts like the Matti-Russe have high failure rates in this setting.

items.q: In the mechanics of the proximal carpal row, the lunate acts as an intercalated segment. Which of the following statements correctly describes the inherent rotational tendencies of the adjacent bones?
o: The scaphoid tends to extend and the triquetrum tends to flex
The scaphoid tends to flex and the triquetrum tends to extend
Both the scaphoid and triquetrum tend to flex
Both the scaphoid and triquetrum tend to extend
items.e: The scaphoid has an inherent tendency to flex, while the triquetrum has an inherent tendency to extend. The lunate is balanced between these opposing forces by the scapholunate and lunotriquetral ligaments.

items.q: On CT reconstructed along the long axis of the scaphoid in a patient with a waist non-union, which of the following measurements indicates a significant 'humpback' (flexion) deformity?
items.e: A height-to-length ratio above 0.65 (and a lateral intrascaphoid angle above about 35-45 degrees) indicates humpback deformity; the other values lie within normal limits.

items.q: A 26-year-old motorcyclist sustains a high-energy wrist hyperextension injury. Lateral radiograph demonstrates that the lunate is tilted and extruded volarly into the carpal tunnel ('spilled teacup' sign) due to failure of the dorsal radiolunate ligament, and the patient displays acute median nerve compression. According to the Mayfield classification, this injury corresponds to:
items.e: Mayfield Stage IV perilunar instability represents true lunate dislocation, where the dorsal radiolunate ligament fails and the lunate is extruded volarly into the carpal tunnel ('spilled teacup sign'), frequently causing acute median nerve compression.

items.q: According to the Geissler arthroscopic classification of scapholunate interosseous ligament tears, which of the following findings defines a Grade III injury?
o: Incongruity and step-off visible in both radiocarpal and midcarpal joints, with a probe able to pass between the bones
Attenuation and hemorrhage of the ligament without carpal incongruity
Incongruity and step-off visible from the midcarpal space only, without a gap admitting the probe
Gross separation of the bones allowing a 2.7 mm arthroscope to pass through the joint space
items.e: Geissler Grade III shows step-off in both radiocarpal and midcarpal joints with a probe passing between scaphoid and lunate. Grade IV is gross instability with the 2.7 mm arthroscope passing through ('drive-through sign').

items.q: A 31-year-old athlete presents with ulnar-sided wrist pain following a fall onto an extended and radially deviated wrist. Radiographs suggest a volar intercalated segment instability (VISI) pattern. Which of the following pairs of provocative physical examination tests is specifically used to evaluate for lunotriquetral dissociation?
o: Watson scaphoid shift test and Finkelstein test
Lichtman midcarpal shift test and Eichhoff test
Durkan carpal compression test and Phalen test
Reagan ballottement test and Kleinman shear test
items.e: Lunotriquetral dissociation is clinically evaluated using specific provocative maneuvers including the Reagan ballottement test, Kleinman shear test, and Derby test. Watson test evaluates scapholunate dissociation, while Lichtman test evaluates midcarpal instability.

items.q: A 32-year-old chef presents 2 days after a fish-bone puncture of the index finger with fusiform swelling, a semi-flexed posture, tenderness along the flexor sheath and severe pain on passive extension. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral antibiotics, splintage and review in 48 hours
Aspiration of the sheath and intra-sheath antibiotic instillation only
Surgical drainage of the flexor sheath (proximal and distal incisions with catheter irrigation) plus IV antibiotics
Primary ray amputation of the index finger
items.e: Established pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis with all four Kanavel signs needs urgent surgical sheath drainage and irrigation with IV antibiotics; a trial of IV antibiotics alone is reserved for very early cases presenting within about 24-48 hours.

items.q: A 35-year-old patient presents with marked swelling over the thenar eminence and the first web space, with the thumb held in an abducted position. Which palmar anatomical structure forms the boundary separating the thenar space from the midpalmar space?
o: Oblique septum originating from the third metacarpal
Lateral intermuscular septum of the hypothenar eminence
items.e: The thenar space lies radial to the oblique septum that originates from the third metacarpal, which anatomical boundary separates it from the midpalmar space lying ulnar to the septum.

items.q: A 42-year-old veterinary technician sustains a deep cat puncture bite to the dorsum of the hand. Which of the following statements regarding animal bite pathogens and their management is correct?
o: Pasteurella multocida is inherently resistant to cefalexin and clindamycin monotherapy
Dog bites have a higher overall rate of infection than cat bites
Cat bites typically manifest after a delayed incubation period of 5 to 7 days
First-generation cephalosporins are the primary empiric drug of choice for cat puncture wounds
items.e: Pasteurella multocida, the commonest organism in deep cat bites (which carry a 30-50% infection rate), is inherently resistant to first-generation cephalosporins (cefalexin), clindamycin (alone), flucloxacillin, and erythromycin; amoxicillin-clavulanate is the antibiotic of choice.

items.q: During fasciectomy for Dupuytren disease, the surgeon must carefully dissect the spiral cord to avoid injuring the digital nerve. Which of the following normal anatomical structures contributes to the formation of the spiral cord?
o: Transverse fibres of the palmar aponeurosis
items.e: The spiral cord is formed from the pretendinous band, spiral band, lateral digital sheet and Grayson ligament, and displaces the neurovascular bundle centrally and superficially. Cleland ligament, dorsal to the bundle, is not involved in Dupuytren disease.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis presents with sudden inability to extend her little and ring fingers at the MCP joints. Passive wrist flexion fails to produce extension at the MCP joints (negative tenodesis test). Radiographs show dorsal subluxation of the ulnar head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Extensor tendon subluxation into the ulnar gutter
items.e: Vaughan-Jackson syndrome is the attrition rupture of extensor tendons (EDM first, followed by EDC of little and ring fingers) over a prominent dorsal ulnar head in rheumatoid arthritis. Passive wrist flexion failing to extend the MCPJs (negative tenodesis effect) differentiates tendon rupture from PIN palsy.

items.q: A 55-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with a swan-neck deformity of the middle finger. Clinical examination demonstrates restricted PIP joint flexion when the MCP joint is extended, but full PIP joint flexion when the MCP joint is flexed (positive Bunnell-Littler test). Radiographs show a preserved PIP joint space. According to the Nalebuff classification, what is the stage and key procedure required?
o: Type I; Flexor digitorum superficialis tenodesis
Type III; Lateral band mobilization and dorsal skin release
items.e: Nalebuff Type II swan-neck deformity is characterized by intrinsic tightness, where PIP flexion is limited with the MCP joint extended but flexible when the MCP joint is flexed (positive Bunnell-Littler test). The definitive management requires intrinsic release in addition to Type I procedures.

items.q: Which component of the original McBride procedure was subsequently omitted in the modified McBride procedure to avoid post-operative hallux varus?
items.e: The original McBride included lateral (fibular) sesamoid excision, which carried a high risk of overcorrection into hallux varus; the modified McBride preserves the lateral sesamoid.

items.q: A 30-year-old patient presents with a painful bunionette deformity. Radiographs demonstrate normal fifth metatarsal head shape but an increased 4th-5th intermetatarsal angle of 12 degrees (>8-10 degrees). According to Coughlin's classification, which type of bunionette is present and what is the recommended procedure?
o: Type II; distal chevron osteotomy alone
Type III; diaphyseal oblique or proximal metatarsal osteotomy
Type III; resection of fifth metatarsal base
items.e: Coughlin Type III bunionette is defined by an increased 4th-5th intermetatarsal angle (>8-10 degrees). The recommended treatment is a diaphyseal oblique or proximal fifth metatarsal osteotomy.

items.q: A 58-year-old man with a rigid hindfoot valgus flatfoot deformity (Johnson and Strom Stage III) undergoes triple arthrodesis. Which joint is the 'key joint' of the hindfoot complex, whose isolated fusion eliminates almost all hindfoot motion, and is also the commonest site of non-union after triple arthrodesis?
items.e: Isolated talonavicular fusion abolishes almost all subtalar and transverse tarsal motion, making it the key joint of the hindfoot; it is also the commonest site of non-union after triple arthrodesis.

items.q: A 28-year-old skier presents with acute lateral ankle pain after a forceful dorsiflexion injury with sudden peroneal contraction. Radiographs demonstrate a small bony "fleck sign" avulsed from the posterolateral fibrocartilaginous rim of the lateral malleolus. According to the Eckert-Davis classification for superior peroneal retinaculum (SPR) injuries, this represents:
items.e: In the Eckert-Davis classification for peroneal tendon subluxation/dislocation, Grade 3 is defined as a bony avulsion fracture of the posterolateral fibular rim (the pathognomonic "fleck sign"). Grade 1 is SPR stripped from fibular periosteum, Grade 2 is elevated fibrocartilaginous rim, and Grade 4 is SPR torn from its calcaneal attachment.

items.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with persistent pain along the lateral midfoot over the cuboid tunnel. Serial lateral foot radiographs demonstrate proximal migration of the os peroneum relative to previous films. This radiographic finding is diagnostic of:
o: Complete rupture of the peroneus longus tendon
Eckert-Davis Grade 1 superior peroneal retinaculum avulsion
items.e: Proximal migration of the os peroneum (a sesamoid located within the peroneus longus tendon at the cuboid notch) on serial radiographs indicates a complete rupture of the peroneus longus tendon, a core feature of Painful Os Peroneum Syndrome (POPS).

items.q: A 58-year-old diabetic male presents with a deep, full-thickness neuropathic ulcer on the plantar surface of the foot that extends down to expose the flexor hallucis longus tendon. There is no local abscess, osteomyelitis, or septic arthritis. According to the Meggitt-Wagner classification system, this ulcer is categorized as:
items.e: Under the Meggitt-Wagner system, Grade 1 is a superficial ulcer involving only skin and subcutaneous tissue; Grade 2 is a deep ulcer penetrating to tendon, capsule, or bone without abscess or osteomyelitis; Grade 3 involves deep tissues with abscess, osteomyelitis, or septic arthritis; and Grade 4 is localized forefoot or toe gangrene.

items.q: A 66-year-old diabetic patient with a chronic forefoot ulcer has an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) of 1.45 due to Mönckeberg medial arterial calcification. Which non-invasive vascular finding best indicates adequate perfusion for ulcer healing?
items.e: Calcified, non-compressible tibial vessels falsely elevate ankle pressures and ABI, so toe pressures (spared calcification) are used; a toe pressure above about 30-40 mmHg or TcPO2 above 30-40 mmHg predicts healing.

items.q: A diabetic patient presents with an erythematous, warm, swollen foot without an ulcer. Which examination finding favours acute Charcot neuroarthropathy rather than cellulitis?
o: Erythema that persists unchanged after 1 minute of limb elevation
Presence of a deep sinus tract probing to bone
Skin temperature difference of less than 0.5 °C compared with the opposite foot
Erythema that resolves within about a minute of limb elevation (Brodsky test)
items.e: In acute Charcot foot the rubor is from neuropathic hyperaemia and fades on elevation, whereas infective erythema persists; a temperature difference of more than 2 °C is typical of active Charcot.

items.q: A patient returns for follow-up 8 weeks after undergoing ORIF for a displaced talar neck fracture. An AP radiograph of the ankle shows a subchondral radiolucent band in the talar dome. What does this finding indicate regarding the prognosis?
o: Impending collapse due to avascular necrosis
Successful revascularization of the talar body
items.e: The Hawkins sign is a subchondral lucency in the talar dome seen at 6-8 weeks post-injury. It represents bone resorption, which implies an intact blood supply and successful revascularization, serving as a good prognostic sign.

items.q: A 52-year-old man presents with anterior ankle impingement and loss of dorsiflexion one year after a calcaneal fracture. Imaging shows a horizontal talus and marked loss of calcaneal height. Which procedure restores talar declination and hindfoot height?
items.e: Loss of calcaneal height leaves a horizontal talus with anterior tibiotalar impingement; subtalar bone-block distraction arthrodesis restores height and talar declination while fusing the arthritic subtalar joint.

items.q: In the management of a high-grade osteosarcoma of the distal femur, the resected specimen after neoadjuvant chemotherapy shows 95% tumour necrosis. According to the Huvos (Rosen-Huvos) grading system, this is classified as:
items.e: Huvos Grade III is defined as 90-99% necrosis and is considered a 'good responder' to chemotherapy. Grade IV is 100% necrosis, while Grades I and II are poor responders.

items.q: A 12-year-old boy with known hereditary multiple exostoses (HME) presents with a shortened ulna, a bowed radius, and a dislocated radial head. There is no osteochondroma identified in the proximal radius. According to the Masada classification, this forearm deformity is categorized as:
items.e: Masada Type IIb is characterized by radial head dislocation secondary to a short ulna (due to a distal ulnar lesion) without a concomitant proximal radial osteochondroma. Type IIa involves a proximal radial lesion.

items.q: Regarding the use of Denosumab in the management of giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB), which of the following statements is true based on current evidence and clinical trials?
o: It is the first-line treatment for all Campanacci Grade II lesions prior to curettage
It effectively kills the neoplastic stromal cells, leading to permanent cure
Neoadjuvant use before curettage is associated with a higher risk of local recurrence
It is contraindicated in patients with pulmonary metastases
items.e: Neoadjuvant denosumab can make curettage more difficult because the resulting peripheral rim of thick new bone can hide residual neoplastic stromal cells (which are not killed by the drug), leading to higher recurrence rates. It is currently recommended for unresectable or metastatic disease, rather than routine use before curettage.

items.q: A 14-year-old girl with precocious puberty and 'coast of Maine' café-au-lait spots has a progressive varus deformity of the proximal femur (Shepherd's crook deformity). What is the preferred definitive surgical management?
o: Curettage and autologous cancellous bone grafting
Bisphosphonate therapy alone until skeletal maturity
En bloc resection and megaprosthetic replacement
Valgus osteotomy with cephalomedullary nail fixation
items.e: This is McCune-Albright syndrome with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia; Shepherd's crook is corrected by valgus osteotomy stabilised with a load-sharing cephalomedullary nail. Cancellous autograft is resorbed and replaced by dysplastic bone.

items.q: According to the Lodwick classification of bone lesion margins, a 'geographic lytic lesion with a well-defined margin but no sclerotic rim' is classified as:
items.e: Grade IA has a sclerotic rim (slow growing). Grade IB is geographic and well-defined but lacks a sclerotic rim (e.g., GCT, Myeloma). Grade IC has ill-defined margins, while Grade II shows a moth-eaten appearance.

items.q: A respiratory therapist has clustered clear vesicles on an erythematous base on the tip of her thumb, preceded by tingling and intense pain. Which of the following is contraindicated in her management?
o: Tzanck smear or PCR of vesicle fluid
items.e: This is herpetic whitlow; incision and drainage is contraindicated as it risks bacterial superinfection and viral dissemination. It is self-limiting and treated with protection and antivirals.

items.q: A 40-year-old manual labourer presents with a 'collar-button' (web space) abscess. On examination, the adjacent fingers are abducted and there is significant swelling on both the volar and dorsal aspects of the web. What is the correct surgical approach for drainage?
o: Single transverse incision across the palmar web
High lateral mid-axial incision on the adjacent finger
items.e: A collar-button abscess is a dumbbell-shaped infection with volar and dorsal components connected through the palmar fascia. Drainage requires dual incisions (volar and dorsal) to address both compartments; incisions should never cross the web space itself to avoid contracture.

items.q: When evaluating suspected necrotising fasciitis of the upper limb, which of the following laboratory parameters is NOT a component of the LRINEC score?
items.e: LRINEC uses CRP, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; ESR is not included.

items.q: A 22-year-old painter sustains a high-pressure injection injury of oil-based paint to his non-dominant index finger. Despite an innocuous-looking entry wound, what is the approximate reported amputation rate for oil-based paint injections?
items.e: Oil-based paints and solvents cause intense chemical inflammation and necrosis with amputation rates of around 50-60%, versus about 6% for water-based paint; urgent wide debridement (ideally within 6 hours) improves outcome.

items.q: In the pathoanatomy of hallux valgus, lateral drift of the hallux and medial drift of the first metatarsal head lead to altered muscle mechanics. Which muscle plantarly migrates, losing its abduction power and acting as a flexor and pronator of the hallux?
items.e: As hallux valgus progresses, the abductor hallucis muscle migrates plantarly relative to the metatarsal head, losing its lateral-to-medial abduction pull and instead acting as a flexor and pronator (evertor) of the hallux.

items.q: A 48-year-old runner presents with pain and stiffness of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint during push-off. Physical examination demonstrates preserved motion with pain only at the extremes of dorsiflexion, and no pain during mid-range motion (negative grind test). Radiographs reveal mild joint space narrowing and a prominent dorsal metatarsal osteophyte (Coughlin and Shurnas Grade 1/2 hallux rigidus). What is the operative procedure of choice?
items.e: Cheilectomy (excision of the dorsal osteophyte and upper 25-30% of the metatarsal head) is indicated for Grade 1 and 2 hallux rigidus with pain restricted to extreme dorsiflexion. First MTP joint arthrodesis is reserved for advanced stage 3 and 4 disease with mid-range pain.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman complains of burning pain in her forefoot that radiates into her third and fourth toes, described as 'walking on a pebble'. Mediolateral compression of the metatarsal heads combined with direct pressure over the third web space produces a palpable click and pain. What is the name of this sign, and where is the lesion located relative to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament?
o: Sullivan sign; proximal to the ligament
Mulder click; distal to the ligament
Lachman test; proximal to the ligament
Silfverskiöld test; distal to the ligament
items.e: A Mulder click is elicited by squeezing the forefoot mediolaterally while pressing the affected intermetatarsal web space, representing a Morton neuroma (perineural fibrosis of the common digital nerve located distal to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament).

items.q: A patient with bilateral cavus foot deformity from Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease presents with severe lesser toe deformities. Clinical examination reveals hyperextension at the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint, flexion at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, and flexion at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Which deformity is described?
items.e: A claw toe is characterised by MTP joint hyperextension, PIP joint flexion, and DIP joint flexion. It is usually bilateral, affects multiple toes, and is commonly caused by intrinsic weakness in neuromuscular disorders or cavus feet.

items.q: During a Scarf osteotomy (Z-shaped diaphyseal osteotomy) for moderate hallux valgus, failure of technical execution leads to telescoping of the diaphyseal cortical bone fragments into one another. Which complication directly results from this structural compromise?
o: Hallux varus due to overcorrection of the intermetatarsal angle
Troughing resulting in metatarsal head elevation and loss of height
Avascular necrosis due to injury to the first dorsal metatarsal artery
items.e: Troughing occurs during a Scarf osteotomy when the cortical fragments telescope into the softer cancellous bone of the metatarsal shaft. This results in loss of height and elevation of the metatarsal head (elevatus), leading to transfer metatarsalgia.

items.q: An American football player sustains a severe hyperdorsiflexion injury to the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint on artificial turf. Examination shows marked vertical instability (positive MTP Lachman test), and plain radiographs confirm proximal migration of the sesamoids with sesamoid diastasis (Grade III turf toe). What is the appropriate definitive management?
o: Nonsurgical management with a metatarsal pad and boot immobilisation
Surgical repair of the plantar plate complex
items.e: Grade III turf toe involves a complete rupture of the plantar capsuloligamentous complex (plantar plate), causing sesamoid diastasis, proximal sesamoid displacement, and vertical MTP instability (positive Lachman test). Grade III injuries require surgical repair of the plantar plate.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with medial ankle pain and flattening of the medial longitudinal arch. Clinical examination demonstrates forefoot abduction ('too many toes' sign from behind). Which physical examination maneuver is the most sensitive test for detecting tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction?
items.e: The single-limb heel rise test is the most sensitive physical examination test for tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction. Patients are either unable to perform a single-limb heel rise or fail to demonstrate normal inversion of the hindfoot on heel rise.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman presents with progressive medial ankle pain and flatfoot deformity. Weight-bearing radiographs show a Meary angle of 20 degrees convex plantar and 45% talonavicular uncoverage. On clinical examination, the hindfoot valgus is completely flexible. Which operative procedure combination is most appropriate?
o: Isolated tenosynovectomy of the tibialis posterior tendon
Flexor digitorum longus transfer to the navicular with medializing calcaneal osteotomy and lateral column lengthening
items.e: This patient has Stage IIB adult acquired flatfoot / progressive collapsing foot deformity (flexible flatfoot with forefoot abduction and >30-40% talonavicular uncoverage). Joint-sparing reconstruction combining flexor digitorum longus (FDL) transfer to the navicular, medializing displacement calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO), and lateral column lengthening (Evans osteotomy) is the treatment of choice.

items.q: A 48-year-old patient undergoes an Evans lateral column lengthening osteotomy as part of a joint-sparing reconstruction for a flexible flatfoot deformity. Which of the following is the most common complication specifically associated with lateral column lengthening?
o: Lateral column overload and lateral foot pain
Tarsal tunnel syndrome from tibial nerve traction
Deltoid ligament rupture causing severe ankle valgus
items.e: Lateral column overload resulting in lateral foot pain is the most common complication of lateral column lengthening (Evans osteotomy or calcaneocuboid distraction arthrodesis).
